Vogue editor-in-chief Anna Wintour watches a model walk the runway on Sept. 14, 2004. (Bryan Bedder/Getty Images)
Wintour "doesn’t understand what people are talking about and thought she could shoulder through this, and it would blow over," another source said.
"Anna’s lost her touch on the zeitgeist," the source said.

Yet insiders said Wintour’s backing of Galliano grew out of her belief in redemption and second chances. Her support for Galliano as the original choice for the 2027 Met Gala wasn't necessarily a surprise.

"It comes from a place of love and forgiveness," an insider told the outlet. "She really believes in people’s second chances and becoming better people and learning from mistakes. It came from a good place. She considers him a friend and wants what’s best for him."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Anna Wintour attends the 2026 Met Gala. (Kevin Mazur/MG26/Getty Images for The Met Museum/Vogue)
"Anna is a big proponent of second chances and getting behind the underdog," another source said.

The source pointed out that Wintour brought Georgina Chapman back into the fashion fold after the #MeToo movement focused attention on allegations against her then-husband, Harvey Weinstein, encouraging people to wear her designer brand, Marchesa.
The insider added, "There is no question Galliano is talented.

"To let him come back is one thing," the source noted. "But to celebrate him on such a scale, especially when antisemitism is at its highest … it sends all the wrong messages. But Anna is very loyal to the people she is loyal to."

title: Dolly Parton's Hollywood Walk of Fame star vandalized days after she was laid to rest

story: Dolly Parton, the Grammy-winning singer, songwriter and philanthropist whose career spanned over six decades, has died at 80.
Dolly Parton’s Hollywood Walk of Fame star was vandalized with multiple scratches, just days after the country music icon was laid to rest.
A fan who visited the star reported the damage on social media. Based on a photo shared by the fan, the star appeared to have been scratched.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Ana Martinez, producer of the Hollywood Walk of Fame, said, "A fan went to the star yesterday and reported on social that the star was vandalized with many scratches.  From the photo she posted, it does appear the star was vandalized with scratches."

Martinez noted that flowers placed at Parton’s star had been removed the morning before the damage was reported as part of a scheduled repair that had been arranged late last week.

"The crew just completed the first part of making said repairs," Martinez said. "The star repairs are currently ongoing and are done by the Hollywood Historic Trust, which maintains and repairs the Walk of Fame stars."
The star is expected to be repaired before being polished Friday, when fans will once again be able to visit the landmark to honor the late singer.

The singer’s niece, Lainey Mae Parton, shared an emotional tribute after her grandmother’s burial, remembering the country legend as a source of unconditional love and support.

title: Dolly Parton prayed in backyard church before recording comeback album, Ricky Skaggs says
summary: Ricky Skaggs reveals how he and Dolly Parton prayed at a tiny rebuilt church in her backyard before recording their hit album "White Limozeen."
story: Country star Ricky Skaggs recalls how Dolly Parton took him inside a church rebuilt at her home, where they prayed before recording her 1989 album "White Limozeen."

Ricky Skaggs is recalling how he and Dolly Parton prayed at the altar of a tiny church rebuilt in her backyard before recording the country comeback album that would help return her to the top of the charts.
During an interview with Fox News Digital, the 72-year-old bluegrass and country star remembered working on 1989's "White Limozeen" with the late music icon, who died on Aug. 25 at the age of 80.
Prior to making "White Limozeen," Skaggs told Fox News Digital that he visited Parton at her home in Nashville, where the two shared a private, faith-filled moment.
DOLLY PARTON'S LIFE IN HER OWN WORDS: FROM SMOKY MOUNTAINS POVERTY TO COUNTRY MUSIC IMMORTALITY

"She took me out in the backyard and showed me this little church that she used to go to when she was a kid up in East Tennessee. They had torn it down and they numbered all the slats and all the flooring and everything like that. They brought it down to her backyard and rebuilt it into a beautiful little church," Skaggs recalled.
Ricky Skaggs recalled praying with Dolly Parton before recording her hit comeback country album. (Country Music Television/Courtesy Everett Collection)

"She wanted me to go in," he continued. "We went in there and they had a little piano in there and a little altar, just like the old Baptist churches in the mountains. So we got up by the altar and just started praying after talking in there for a while about our faith. And we asked God’s hand to be on this record, that he would bless it, bless the musicians, bless all the singers."
CARRIE UNDERWOOD HONORS DOLLY PARTON'S FAITH AND LEGACY DURING EMOTIONAL CONCERT TRIBUTE
"I just never have forgotten just the power of that day," Skaggs added. "That whole day was just wonderful. It showed me the kind of woman she was."

Skaggs recalled how he teamed up with Parton on "White Limozeen" after she invited him to produce the album following an appearance by the singer and his country band on her Los Angeles-based television show "Dolly."
WATCH: DOLLY PARTON PRAYED AT BACKYARD ALTAR BEFORE COMEBACK ALBUM, RICKY SKAGGS SAYS
DOLLY PARTON DEFIED COUNTRY MUSIC'S EXPECTATIONS FOR WOMEN AND BUILT A CAREER ON HER OWN TERMS: EXPERTS
"I came up and hugged her 'bye' and told her I really appreciate her having us on the show. And I said, ‘By the way, when are you going to do a real country album again?’" he remembered.
Skaggs continued, "She said, ‘Well, I’ve been thinking a lot about that. And I think I really want to do a country record. But I want you to produce it.’ I said, ‘What?'"
STEVE DOOCY: THE DOLLY PARTON I SAW WHEN THE CAMERAS STOPPED ROLLING

"I was shocked to the bone," he admitted. "That was one of the most mind-blowing, waking up smelling the roses kind of thing that I'd ever had happen at that time, musically for sure. But that was just being the right person in the right place at the right time around the right person."
"Only God could make those things happen."
Parton invited Skaggs to produce her album after he and his band appeared on her TV show. (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
DOLLY PARTON'S MOST ICONIC 'DOLLY-ISMS' ON BEAUTY, WIGS, BOTOX AND LIVING LIFE ON HER OWN TERMS

After rising to global fame as a country singer, Parton spent much of the late 1970s and 1980s broadening into pop-influenced material. Prior to "White Limozeen," she released her 1987 solo album "Rainbow," which was a critical and commercial disappointment. "Rainbow," which marked her most overtly pop-leaning solo album, struggled to find an audience, peaking at No. 18 on Billboard’s Top Country Albums and failing to produce a Top 40 country single.

With "White Limozeen," Skaggs brought Parton back to a more traditional country sound. The album became a hit, reaching No. 3 on Billboard’s Top Country Albums chart, yielding two No. 1 country hits, "Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That" and "Yellow Roses," and earning a Gold certification from the RIAA.
DOLLY PARTON'S BELOVED LITERACY MISSION SEES SURGE OF SUPPORT AFTER COUNTRY ICON'S DEATH
Although "White Limozeen" remained their only major recording collaboration, Skaggs said he and Parton shared a lasting bond rooted in their Appalachian backgrounds and Christian faith.
The Kentucky native said Parton lived out her beliefs through compassion and generosity, even though some were critical of her glamorous image.
"White Limozeen" became a hit and produced two No. 1 singles. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
BROADCAST BIAS: DOLLY PARTON TAUGHT THE WORLD THE WAY TO BE UNIVERSALLY BELOVED

"Some religious people would have really, and probably did, judge her for the way she wore her clothes, or the way that she did this and that and the other, but man, she reflected the love of Jesus everywhere she was," he said. "She did so much for the homeless, for the poor, for hurting people."

"She used what God had given her with her talent and her gifts, but she used that for His advantage, I mean, to show God's love to people that didn't feel loved by the world or by others, even other Christians," Skaggs continued. "And I just, I loved her for that. And I've really thought a lot about that since her passing."
BIG & RICH SAY DOLLY PARTON PUT FAME ASIDE TO HELP NEIGHBORS AFTER 2016 TENNESSEE WILDFIRES

Throughout her life, Parton was known for her philanthropy, which spanned literacy, disaster relief and medical research. In 1995, she launched the Imagination Library, a program that gifted hundreds of millions of free, age-appropriate books to children from birth to age 5 worldwide.

The 11-time Grammy Award winner also established the My People Fund after the 2016 Great Smoky Mountains wildfires, providing eligible Sevier County families whose homes were destroyed with $1,000 a month for up to six months. In 2020, Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center for COVID-19 research.
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Skaggs reflected on how the moment he shared with Parton in her backyard church had stayed with him and influenced his own band's pre-show ritual.
Skaggs said he was inspired by Parton, and he and his band pray before every performance. (Getty Images)

"Me and my band nowadays, we pray every time before we go out on stage and everything," he said. "We just say a prayer and thank God for our gifts and our talents and just ask that someone would be touched by the songs that we do."

"I just never have forgotten just the power of that day," he added. "That whole day was wonderful. It showed me the kind of woman that she was."
Skaggs also shared how he hoped that Parton would be remembered following her death.
"She was serious about music. She was serious about her life. She was serious about God," he said. "I'm telling you in her heart, I never met a person that had a more pure golden heart than Dolly."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Skaggs said Parton had a "pure golden heart." (Getty Images)
"She was pure hearted," Skaggs added. "I never heard her judge anyone."

The "Country Boy" singer told Fox News Digital that he believed Parton's dedication to philanthropy would also be a major part of her lasting legacy.

"We don’t even know what all that she’s done," he said. "Probably her family does, but she told them, ‘Look, don’t be out telling all the things I’m doing. I don’t want people to think I’m doing this for publicity. I don’t need it. I don’t want it. I want to do this because I love people and I want to help.’"

title: Prince William, Kate Middleton face 'Sussex circus' as Prince George prepares for Eton: expert
summary: Prince George is set to start at Eton College, but the Sussexes' return to the U.K. has royal commentators warning of competing headlines and tension.
story: Fox News contributor Raymond Arroyo discusses Prince Harry and Meghan Markle returning to the United Kingdom on 'The Ingraham Angle.'

While Prince William and Princess Kate's attention is focused on Prince George's approaching move to Eton, Prince Harry and Duchess Meghan's return to the U.K. could introduce a new source of family tension, according to royal experts.
George, 13, is expected to begin at Eton College this month, marking a major milestone for the Prince and Princess of Wales as their eldest child prepares to leave home for boarding school.

The occasion comes as Harry and Meghan have returned to the U.K. with their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. However, according to royal experts, the couple is expected to avoid making public comments or releasing photos that could overshadow George's first day.
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON COULD SEEK 'GENTLEMAN'S AGREEMENT' TO PROTECT PRINCE GEORGE AT ETON: EXPERTS
Prince William, Princess Kate brace for "unpredictability" with Meghan Markle and Prince Harry's return as Prince George starts Eton, an expert says. (Getty Images)
Still, royal commentator Kinsey Schofield told Fox News Digital that the Sussexes' presence could create an unpredictable wave of emotions for the Wales family during an already trying time.

"I have tremendous sympathy for the Prince and Princess of Wales," Schofield said. "Prince George is expected to start at Eton on September 8, which means this was their last Scottish summer holiday together before their teenage son leaves home for his first term at boarding school."
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON WRESTLED WITH MAJOR DECISION OVER PRINCE GEORGE'S FUTURE: EXPERT
"That is a huge emotional milestone for any family, and instead of being able to quietly enjoy that time together, Harry and Meghan have brought the circus back to town," she added.
Schofield said William and Kate may be forced to navigate the media attention surrounding Harry and Meghan while trying to maintain privacy for their children.
PRINCE WILLIAM ‘BLINDSIDED’ BY HARRY, MEGHAN RETURN AS KATE FEARS NEW TURMOIL FROM ROYAL FEUD: EXPERTS
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have vowed to "lay low" amid their U.K. return and Prince George's Eton start, according to a royal expert. (Getty Images)

"What I think will be particularly difficult for William and Catherine is the unpredictability," Schofield said. "Harry and Meghan have a history of making their own plans, generating enormous media attention and operating outside the traditional royal structure."

"Now William and Catherine are sending their eldest child away from home for the first time while simultaneously having to navigate the Sussexes' return and all of the uncertainty surrounding it," she added.
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE'S UK RETURN SIGNALS ‘SPECTACULAR DEFEAT’ AS ROYAL EXPERTS WARN OF WILLIAM SHOWDOWN
Schofield said George should be allowed to begin his new chapter without being pulled into the ongoing media frenzy surrounding his family.
"George deserves to begin this new chapter of his life without being dragged into another cycle of speculation about his uncle and aunt," Schofield said.
PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE ARRIVE IN UK WITH KIDS, MARKING DRAMATIC RETURN 6 YEARS AFTER ROYAL EXIT

"William and Catherine have worked incredibly hard to give their children stability and privacy, and I imagine they would have preferred this important family moment to happen without the Sussex circus playing out in the background," she added.
Richard Fitzwilliams, a royal commentator, said the Sussexes' return could intensify the pressure on the royal family and the Palace.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle and their two children returned to the U.K. last week. (Matt Dunham - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY

"The royal family is under pressure," Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "The Palace is not at its best reacting to the unexpected, and the Sussexes know that, hence this strange game they seem to be playing."
Fitzwilliams also questioned whether Harry and Meghan's return signals a genuine commitment to Britain or reflects their efforts to maintain an international profile.
"They reportedly see themselves as 'international citizens,'" he said. "They claim that their balance of business activities and trips abroad over the last six years is a success."
The couple's arrival in Britain has also drawn attention to their public image and ongoing security concerns.
The Sussexes moved to California in 2020. (Getty Images)
"They are making a statement by arriving by private jet," Fitzwilliams said. "Harry is apparently still wanting an apology. He may or may not get the security he craves, or part of it."
"The test ought to be if there is a threat and not public opinion polls," he added.
Fitzwilliams said public opinion remains a challenge for the Sussexes, pointing to YouGov popularity ratings.
"The people would love them to depart, though the circus they create is weird and anthropologically fascinating," he said.

The reported agreement for Harry and Meghan to "lay low" during George's Eton debut was previously described by royal broadcaster Neil Sean as an effort to prevent the Sussexes from overshadowing the future king's historic first day.

"The Sussexes have assured the king that they will not hijack or derail major royal events, notably the first day of school term for Prince George at Eton," Sean previously told Fox News Digital. "By that, no pictures or comment from either one on that day in September."
At the time, a representative for Archewell told Fox News Digital: "This is not something we would comment on."
Royal commentator Amanda Matta previously said George's first day at Eton carries significance beyond a typical school milestone.
Prince George will attend Eton this month. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

"Prince George's start at Eton isn't just a personal milestone; it's the beginning of his public-facing path as heir to the throne," Matta said. "The Palace is incredibly protective of that narrative, and any competing headline — especially one involving Harry and Meghan — threatens to distract from the 'steady, future-focused' brand the Prince and Princess of Wales have worked so hard to build."

Matta added that it would "certainly be a shame for his first days at Eton to see him embroiled in a 'feud' narrative with his uncle and aunt."
Harry and Meghan stepped down as senior working royals in 2020 and later moved to California. They are expected to retain ties to California while re-establishing themselves in Britain.
Schofield described the couple's reported U.K. plans as "a trial run rather than a definitive homecoming."

"The fact that this is apparently not intended to be a permanent move tells us that Harry and Meghan are still hedging their bets," she said. "They are returning to Britain, but they do not appear ready to fully commit to Britain."

title: Deadly mosquito-borne virus claims first life in major US city as cases spread
summary: Chicago's first West Nile virus death of 2026 follows the city's rainiest summer in years, as CDPH sprays insecticide across 15 community areas.
story: Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious diseases and addiction medicine doctor and associate professor at University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine, discusses the spread, symptoms and management of West Nile virus.
A Chicago resident has died from West Nile virus, marking the city’s first death linked to the mosquito-borne illness this year, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health.
Several other cases have been reported throughout Illinois.

The virus is most commonly spread to people through the bite of an infected mosquito, although the disease cycle also includes infected birds. When mosquitoes feed on infected birds, they can pick up the virus and transmit it to humans.
2 AIRPORT WORKERS ARE DEAD AFTER MALARIA CASES SHOCK OFFICIALS AT MAJOR TRAVEL HUB
"2026 has seen the rainiest summer in Chicago in years, giving mosquitoes ample opportunities to breed," CDPH Commissioner Garth Walker said in a statement.
"The best way to protect yourself from West Nile virus is to avoid mosquito bites and take measures to stop them from breeding around your home."
A Chicago resident has died from West Nile virus, marking the city’s first death linked to the mosquito-borne illness this year, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health. (iStock)

In an attempt to prevent infections, the CDPH has sprayed insecticide in the following community areas: Beverly, Burnside, Chatham, East Garfield Park, the Lower West Side, Morgan Park, the Near West Side, North Lawndale, O'Hare, Pullman, Roseland, South Deering, Washington Heights, West Lawn and West Pullman.
Symptoms and treatment
For most people, West Nile produces mild symptoms — such as fever, aches and rashes — or none at all, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
VACATION HOT SPOT FACES NEW CDC TRAVEL WARNING AS OUTBREAK CASES CONTINUE CLIMBING
In rare serious cases, the virus invades the nervous system, causing meningitis, encephalitis (swelling of the brain), paralysis or death.
People over 50 or those with compromised immune systems are at highest risk, experts caution.
West Nile virus is most commonly spread to people through the bite of an infected mosquito, although the disease cycle also includes infected birds.  (iStock)

"Of those who do have symptoms, about 20%, maybe 25%, will have the flu-like symptoms — fever, headache, body aches — and it’s very hard to distinguish between that and flu," Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious diseases and addiction medicine doctor and associate professor at University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
There are also rare, severe neuroinvasive cases, when the virus infects the brain.
"When there's inflammation that leads to meningitis or encephalitis, that's very bad," warned Evans, who is also the CEO and chief medical officer for Wellness Equity Alliance.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"So if there's ever any severe headaches, stiff neck, disorientation, vision loss, feeling like you're just really confused, and if you're over the age of 65, or have immunocompromising conditions like severe diabetes or cancers, that's when you're going to want to seek emergency management as quickly as possible."
While there are no vaccines or specific treatments for West Nile virus, there are supportive treatments.
For most people, West Nile produces mild symptoms — such as fever, aches and rashes — or none at all, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. (iStock)
"For the flu-like symptoms, generally speaking, if you're not over the age of 65 and you're not immunocompromised, you don't have to go to the emergency room," Evans advised.
"But if you are over the age of 65 and/or have those immunocompromising conditions, and you're starting to experience confusion, headache, stiff neck … ER immediately, [call] 911."
Prevention tips
Avoiding mosquito bites is the first line of defense, according to Evans.
"In areas where there are a lot of mosquitoes, DEET is going to be key," he said, recommending repellents that are at least 30% DEET for adults.
In high-burden mosquito areas, he also recommends avoiding the outdoors during sundown.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Health officials also recommend wearing loose, long-sleeved clothing; applying insect repellent (especially at dawn and dusk when mosquitoes are most active); and ensuring that window screens are secure.
Around homes, eliminating standing water (like that found in buckets, tires and gutters) can help keep mosquitoes from breeding.

There have been 407 reported human cases of West Nile virus in the U.S. this year, including 285 severe neuroinvasive cases and 23 deaths, according to the latest preliminary CDC data, current as of Sept. 1.
Most West Nile cases are reported in August and September.

title: Popular diet slashes liver fat by 67% while reversing prediabetes in some people
summary: A keto diet reduced liver fat by roughly 67% and reversed prediabetes in half of participants, but the study's small sample size is a caveat.
story: Registered dietitian Ilana Muhlstein discusses research comparing ketogenic, Mediterranean and plant-forward eating patterns, including their effects on hepatic fat, glucose control and metabolic health.
The keto diet may have surprising benefits for liver health, a new study suggests.
The research, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, studied 42 adults who had obesity, prediabetes and excess liver fat.
In a randomized clinical trial, the participants were assigned to three weight-loss diets – a low-carb ketogenic diet, a Mediterranean diet and a low-fat, mostly plant-based diet.
SECRET TO WEIGHT LOSS MAY BE HIDING IN YOUR GUT, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS

The keto diet’s calories consisted of about 4% carbohydrates and 73% fat, according to the study. The Mediterranean diet provided about 50% of calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat, while the low-fat diet provided about 70% of calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.
In all three groups, muscle insulin sensitivity improved by about 50%, helping the muscles take up blood sugar more efficiently.
Liver fat decreased by roughly 67% in those following the keto diet, compared to about 45% with the other diets. (iStock)
Liver insulin sensitivity improved two to three times as much in the keto group as in the other diet groups.

Liver fat decreased by roughly 67% among people following the keto diet, compared with about 45% among those on the other diets. The reduction was linked to a decrease in the liver’s production of new fat.

Glucose and insulin measures also generally improved more in the keto group. About 50% of participants in that group no longer met the criteria for prediabetes by the end of the trial, compared with 29% of those following the Mediterranean diet and 7% of those on the low-fat diet.
ONE COMMON TYPE OF FAT MAY INCREASE DIABETES RISK, WHILE ANOTHER HELPS FIGHT IT
The study’s short duration and small sample size — about 14 people in each diet group — limit how broadly the findings can be applied to the general population, the researchers said.

The researchers concluded that, among people with obesity, prediabetes and excess liver fat, the composition of a weight-loss diet may influence certain metabolic outcomes beyond the effects of weight loss alone. The keto diet produced the greatest improvements in liver fat and liver insulin sensitivity in this small trial.
People on the keto diet saw two to three times greater improvements in how well their liver responded to insulin. (iStock)
Registered dietitian nutritionist Ilana Muhlstein reflected on the study findings.
"I love more and more validation and recognition that calories are not equal," the California-based expert told Fox News Digital.

Muhlstein said people often reduce weight loss to "just a calorie deficit," but this study showed that differences in macronutrients were associated with different changes in health markers despite similar weight loss.
POPULAR DIET TREND COULD BOOST MENTAL HEALTH AMONG OLDER ADULTS, STUDY FINDS

Although weight loss occurred across all three groups, Muhlstein said the participants experienced different internal metabolic changes. The keto group showed a greater reduction in the liver’s production of new fat, along with metabolic changes consistent with greater fat burning.
Anyone with a fatty liver should consider transitioning to a lower carbohydrate diet, a nutritionist advised. (iStock)
Muhlstein explained that excess calories and metabolic dysfunction can cause fat to accumulate in the liver, even in people who do not drink alcohol.
She recommends that anyone with a fatty liver should consider transitioning to a lower carbohydrate diet.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Muhlstein said reducing carbohydrate intake may encourage the body to use more stored fat for energy.
The findings were notable because the keto group did not experience higher cholesterol or blood-fat measurements during the short study, the expert noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"This is a really interesting study for someone who has prediabetes, someone who had blood sugar irregularity, but maybe still something to be cautious of if someone has heart disease in the family or is at high risk of heart disease," she added.
After achieving significant weight loss, the nutritionist recommends transitioning to something closer to the Mediterranean diet for "long-term overall health." (iStock)

Overall, Muhlstein said the findings suggest keto may be worth discussing as a short-term option for some people with obesity or prediabetes, particularly because the study found greater reductions in liver fat and higher rates of prediabetes remission — even though weight loss was similar across the three groups.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Keto is not something I recommend for anyone long-term because of the high saturated fat, and usually it translates into a lower-fiber diet, which is not good for heart health," Muhlstein said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"So potentially, it should be something used short-term early on for someone with prediabetes, and then they can transition into Mediterranean, which would be overall helpful for your heart, your brain and so much more."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Women who start common hormone therapy in their 50s may have 23% lower dementia risk
summary: Hormone replacement therapy started between ages 46 and 56 was tied to lower Alzheimer's and dementia risk, a major new UK Biobank study suggests.
story: Dr. Alexa Fiffick, a board-certified family medicine physician and founder of Concierge Medicine of Westlake in Cleveland, Ohio, speaks about a new study linking hormone replacement therapy to lower dementia risk.
Women who start hormone replacement therapy (HRT) at a certain age may have a lower dementia risk, a new study suggests.
The study, published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia, analyzed UK Biobank data of 183,450 postmenopausal women averaging 60 years of age.
The U.K. researchers determined that HRT use was associated with about a 10% lower risk of all-cause dementia and a 16% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease over a 13-year follow-up period.
'LONGEVITY GENE' MAY PROTECT THE BRAIN FROM ALZHEIMER'S BY BOOSTING DNA REPAIR, STUDY FINDS
The association was strongest among women who started the therapy between the ages of 46 and 56. It was also high among those who had undergone surgical menopause.
Starting HRT after age 56 was not associated with reduced dementia risk.
Women who start hormone replacement therapy at a certain age may have a lower dementia risk, a new study suggests. (iStock)

Dr. Alexa Fiffick, a board-certified family medicine physician and founder of Concierge Medicine of Westlake in Cleveland, Ohio, noted that this was an observational study that can’t show cause and effect.
"So, it kind of stays where the data has been for a while — that in certain patients, we have no evidence that it really makes a difference," she told Fox News Digital.
7 NEW DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS REVEALED — INCLUDING ONE MILLIONS STRUGGLE WITH

"And, for some patients, such as [those] who go through menopause a little bit younger, whether that's surgically or naturally, or if they have that APOE ε4 genotype that predisposes them to dementia, there may be some benefit."
Study limitations
The researchers also stated that since this was an observational study, it could not establish that HRT prevents dementia but only showed an association.
The study also did not assess any safety outcomes or adverse events related to HRT.
Women who use HRT may differ from non-users in other ways that affect dementia risk, such as their overall health, lifestyle or access to healthcare, the researchers noted.
There is some data linking menopausal symptoms, such as hot flashes and night sweats, with vascular changes in the brain, a doctor noted. (iStock)
Although researchers adjusted for many of these factors, some unmeasured differences could still factor into the lower dementia risk seen among HRT users.
The study also did not have detailed information on the types of hormone therapy, the way they were administered or the specific dosages women took.
"If you're having symptoms, if you feel not yourself, come in, talk to your doctor, have that conversation."
Most of the people in the study were of European ancestry and tended to be better off financially, so the findings may not apply equally to people from other populations.
This study alone likely doesn't warrant seeking out HRT just for dementia prevention, Fiffick said.
"However, if you're having symptoms, if you feel not yourself, come in, talk to your doctor, have that conversation," she advised.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
There is some data linking menopausal symptoms, such as hot flashes and night sweats, with vascular changes in the brain, the doctor noted.
"So, we are very hopeful to see that treating those symptoms may prevent the vascular changes that lead to vascular dementia, but we just don't have that data right now," she said.
"So, it's worth the conversation, it's worth bringing up, but I wouldn't go out of your way for just this purpose."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
HRT does carry some known risks and side effects, Fiffick noted.
For oral versions of estrogen, there may be an increased risk of blood clots. That risk does not appear to exist for transdermal options, such as patches, gels and creams.
As this was an observational study, it could not establish that HRT prevents dementia but only showed an association. (iStock)
Other types of HRT may impact breast activity, overall inflammation, cardiovascular markers and cardiometabolic markers, according to the doctor.
"So, it's not one size fits all, and it's really worth an extensive conversation."
Looking ahead

The U.K. researchers plan to conduct randomized controlled trials to confirm that HRT reduces dementia risk. Future studies will include factors such as estrogen-only versus combined therapy, dosage amounts, administration route, treatment duration, age at the start of therapy, menopause type and potentially APOE genotype.

"I think the more we have studies like this, the more we're going to propel forward the randomized controlled trials to really give women the data they deserve," Fiffick concluded.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Women deserve to have information to use to make decisions about their bodies. So I'm excited to see the trends heading in that direction."

title: New weight-loss compound melts fat without curbing appetite — and preserves muscle
summary: University of California, Berkeley scientists found TOFA boosted energy expenditure in obese mice without the lean muscle loss tied to semaglutide.
story: Dr. Leslie Pristas, a bariatric surgeon and owner of Best Life Bariatrics and Medical Weight Loss in Ohio, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential of an experimental obesity therapy.
A team of researchers led by scientists at the University of California, Berkeley, has identified a decades-old oral compound that produced substantial weight loss in obese mice.
Rather than suppressing appetite, the compound appears to boost energy expenditure, according to a study published in Science Advances.
The molecule, known as TOFA, reduced the mice’s body weight by an average of 18% without changing how much they ate or causing a statistically significant loss of lean mass.
NEW OBESITY TREATMENT MAY HELP PRESERVE MUSCLE DURING WEIGHT LOSS

While popular injectable weight-loss medications such as semaglutide can produce substantial weight loss partly by reducing food intake, some patients experience gastrointestinal side effects and loss of lean mass.
Studies have also found that people often regain a significant amount of weight after stopping treatment.
Researchers found that an oral compound called TOFA produced substantial weight loss in obese mice by boosting energy expenditure rather than suppressing appetite like GLP-1s. (iStock)
Preserving muscle during weight loss remains one of the greatest clinical hurdles in obesity medicine, according to experts.

"Muscle mass is really important for our function during the day. It helps fight the effects of aging," Dr. Leslie Pristas, a bariatric surgeon and owner of Best Life Bariatrics and Medical Weight Loss in Northeast Ohio, told Fox News Digital.
"Building muscle is really hard. It takes a really long time. So if we can avoid having muscle loss while we're having weight loss, that's going to be so much better."
THIS COULD BE WHY YOUR WEIGHT-LOSS MEDICATION ISN’T DELIVERING RESULTS

Instead of primarily targeting appetite, TOFA acts inside cells, according to the researchers. It blocks enzymes involved in the production of lipids, including fats such as triglycerides, while also activating cellular receptors that turn on genes involved in fat burning and energy production.
Treated mice burned up to 18% more energy under room-temperature and mildly warm conditions, without becoming less active or developing a dangerous increase in body temperature.
Preserving muscle during weight loss is critical for long-term health, as a bariatric surgeon noted that muscle protects daily physical function and helps combat aging. (iStock)

When the researchers combined TOFA with existing obesity drugs such as semaglutide or tirzepatide, the combination treatments produced greater reductions in body weight and improvements in blood sugar, insulin and triglyceride levels than either drug alone.
Mice treated with TOFA maintained body weights close to control levels after treatment ended, while mice previously given semaglutide began rapidly regaining weight.
PATIENTS TAKING WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS OFTEN MAKE 5 CRITICAL MISTAKES, DOCTOR WARNS
Pristas urged caution against assuming that any single medication could permanently prevent post-treatment weight gain.
"Obesity is super complex," she said. "There's not just one mechanism by which everyone gains weight or even a single person gains weight. There are a lot of overlapping factors."
"If we can avoid having muscle loss while we're having weight loss, that's going to be so much better."

"Once we have extra weight on our body, that kind of becomes where our body thinks we're supposed to be. That becomes our body's weight set point," she noted, adding that if someone stops a medication abruptly, the body may then work to return to its previous weight.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The compound also showed promise in mouse models for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a form of fatty liver disease. Mice given TOFA had less liver fat, inflammation and fibrosis (scarring).
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

TOFA achieved these liver benefits without increasing triglyceride levels in the blood, the researchers noted. Some similar metabolic drugs have caused triglycerides to rise, creating potential cardiovascular and other health concerns that have complicated their development.
Study limitations
The authors emphasized that all the animal experiments involved male mice. Future studies will need to determine whether TOFA produces similar results in female animals.

The drug has not yet been tested in people, so researchers still don't know what dose would be appropriate, whether it is safe to use over long periods, or whether it could cause subtle toxicities or other safety problems.
Patients concerned about their weight-loss journey should speak to a professional before making any medication changes. (iStock)
Pristas emphasized that early mouse data must be weighed carefully against potential hidden side effects in humans.
"If it sounds too good to be true, it's probably too good to be true," she said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"When you're talking about manipulating our bodies' manufacturing or processing of lipids, it's complex. And so there can be downstream effects that we don't want. That's where we can't get too excited."
However, the expert said the treatment could eventually benefit people, either on its own or in combination with another therapy.

title: Teen dies from ‘brain-eating amoeba’ just days after young girl succumbs to same rare infection
summary: A North Carolina teen's first symptom was severe headaches before a brain-eating amoeba infection proved fatal, his mother shared on GoFundMe.
story: Dr. Jeffrey Kahn, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at UT Southwestern and Children's Health in Dallas, Texas, says Naegleria fowleri is very rare, but nearly 100% fatal.

BEACHGOERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY 'FLESH-EATING' BACTERIA KILLS 5 IN SOUTHERN STATE

"We extend our condolences to the family, friends and community impacted by this loss," the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement obtained by news outlets.
A North Carolina teenager has died from a rare and often fatal infection caused by an amoeba found in warm freshwater, state health officials said. (GoFundMe)
The teen’s death was reported just days after an 8-year-old girl in Louisiana succumbed to the infection.

"While these infections are very rare, this is an important reminder that this amoeba is present in our state and across the U.S.," State Epidemiologist Zack Moore, M.D., said in a prior statement. "There are steps people can take to reduce their risk of infection while swimming during the warmer months."
DOCTORS THOUGHT MAN HAD BRAIN CANCER — THEY FOUND LIVE TAPEWORMS INSTEAD
Naegleria fowleri — commonly referred to as a "brain-eating amoeba" — causes a life-threatening brain infection called primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM).
The amoeba is most active in the months that the water temperature stays elevated.

"It's typically this time of year when it's very hot outside, when there hasn't been a lot of rain … and the lakes and ponds get pretty stagnant and get very warm, and that's a great breeding ground for these type of natural inhabitants of those waters," Dr. Jeffrey Kahn, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at UT Southwestern and Children's Health in Dallas, Texas, told Fox News Digital.
A microscopic image shows Naegleria fowleri, the amoeba that causes the rare brain infection primary amoebic meningoencephalitis. (CDC)

The infection can occur when water containing the amoeba is forced up the nose, allowing the amoeba to travel to the brain. This can occur when someone jumps or dives into the water or participates in water sports.
"Once that happens, it's nearly a lethal disease," Kahn warned. "The mortality rate is close to 100%."
Naegleria fowleri does not cause illness via swallowing.
Warning signs to recognize
The initial symptoms of PAM usually begin about five days after exposure, but they can be noticed sooner.
Early signs usually include headache, nausea, fever and/or vomiting, the CDC’s website states.
As the infection progresses, people may experience confusion, slurred speech, stiff neck, disorientation, hallucinations, seizures and coma.
"By the time the [amoeba] enters the brain and starts to basically erode the brain tissue, it's too late."
"The initial symptoms are actually quite nonspecific — they don't point to one disease or another — but they can progress very rapidly," Kahn noted.
Diagnosis involves testing cerebrospinal fluid obtained through a spinal tap; specialized laboratory testing may be needed.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Symptoms usually begin about five days after exposure, although they can appear anywhere from one to 12 days later. Once symptoms start, the disease progresses rapidly.
Most people die within one to 18 days after symptoms begin, typically around five days, per the CDC.
Prevention of infection
To prevent potentially fatal infections, Kahn recommends either avoiding the types of waters where the amoeba is likelier to be found, or taking added precautions.
The amoeba is most active in the months that the water temperature stays elevated. (iStock)
"If you are swimming in those waters, wear a nose clip, don't put your head underwater, those types of things," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Drinking contaminated water does not present a risk, and the infection does not spread from one person to another.
Because the amoeba is found in soil, the CDC also recommends avoiding stirring up the sediment at the bottom of lakes, ponds and rivers.
Treatment of brain-eating amoebas

When a patient has been diagnosed with a brain-eating amoeba, treatment involves a combination of antimicrobial and anti-amoebic medications, including amphotericin B, azithromycin, rifampin and miltefosine.

"There has been a cocktail of antibiotics and antimicrobials that have been tried over the years — but with a very, very small number of cases every year, it's tough to draw any conclusions from that," Kahn said.

"In the cases we've seen, we typically throw a lot of these antibiotics as a therapeutic modality, but by the time the [amoeba] enters the brain and starts to basically erode the brain tissue, it's too late."

Those who experience sudden headache, fever, stiff neck or vomiting — especially if they have recently been swimming in warm freshwater — should seek immediate medical attention, the CDC recommends.

title: 7 new dementia risk factors revealed — including one millions struggle with
summary: The World Health Organization has added seven new dementia risk factors, including stroke, sleep apnea, HIV and air pollution, to its updated guidelines.
story: Psychiatrist Daniel Amen discusses updated global recommendations for reducing cognitive decline, highlighting hormones, cardiovascular health, restorative rest, sensory loss, social connection and other factors tied to healthy aging.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has released a major update to its guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.
The second edition of the original 2019 report was updated to "reflect the latest evidence and advances in dementia risk reduction."
The following seven additional health conditions and exposures were added to the list.
LEARNING ANOTHER LANGUAGE MAY KEEP YOUR BRAIN YOUNGER, STUDY SUGGESTS
Stroke
Traumatic brain injury
Vision impairment
Sleep problems
HIV
Air pollution
Menopausal hormone therapy
The WHO's updated guidelines "reflect the latest evidence and advances in dementia risk reduction." (iStock)
These new risk factors joined the previously existing 12, which are listed below.
Cognitive activity
Social activity
Physical inactivity
Harmful alcohol use
Tobacco use
Unhealthy diet/nutrition
Obesity
Diabetes
Hypertension
Dyslipidemia (abnormal amount of lipids (fats) or lipoproteins in the blood)
Hearing loss
Depression
WARDING OFF ALZHEIMER'S MIGHT MEAN MAKING THESE 11 LIFESTYLE CHANGES, EXPERT SAYS
Dr. Daniel Amen, physician and founder of Amen Clinics in California, has his own formula for reducing Alzheimer’s risk factors, following an acronym called BRIGHT MINDS.

This stands for blood flow, retirement and aging, inflammation, genetics, head trauma, toxins, mental health, immunity and infections, neurohormones, diabesity (co-occurrence of obesity and type 2 diabetes) and sleep. The WHO’s updated guidelines offer similar advice.
Menopausal hormone therapy is primarily used to treat symptoms of menopause. (iStock)
Amen spoke with Fox News Digital about the new additions to the WHO's list of risk factors.
Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT)

The WHO does not recommend menopausal hormone therapy specifically to prevent dementia in postmenopausal women 65 and older. For younger women, it says there is not enough evidence to determine whether MHT affects dementia risk.

Amen agreed that there is not enough evidence to support using MHT specifically to prevent dementia. He said hormonal changes during menopause may affect mood and memory, although the relationship between MHT and dementia risk remains uncertain.
'I'M A NEUROLOGIST — HERE'S WHY DEMENTIA IS RISING AND HOW TO REDUCE YOUR RISK’

"For women, as they go through menopause, lower progesterone makes them anxious, and [with] lower estrogen, they start to have memory problems," he said. "Hormone replacement early on is helpful, and that's what we see on the brain imaging work that we do."
Experts note that while menopause-related hormonal changes can be associated with mood and cognitive symptoms, these effects can vary widely.
Stroke
A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in or near the brain bursts, according to the American Stroke Association.
Conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels can also affect brain health and are associated with a higher risk of dementia, according to Amen.
Any blood flow blockages can impact brain health and increase the risk of dementia. (iStock)
That can include conditions such as heart disease, heart rhythm problems, stroke and transient ischemic attacks. Erectile dysfunction can also be associated with underlying vascular disease, he said.
"And 40% of 40-year-olds have erectile dysfunction, 70% of 70-year-olds. So, if I'm an older person, I'm thinking if I get my brain right, my love life could be better, too," Amen added.
Traumatic brain injury (TBI)
Amen surmised that the WHO is "late to the party" in emphasizing the importance of head trauma as a dementia risk factor. TBI can range from a mild concussion to a severe brain injury.
COMMON VACCINE LINKED TO 24% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK IN OLDER ADULTS

"One of the big lessons from the brain imaging work we do is that mild traumatic brain injury ruins people's lives," he said. "They end up seeing psychiatrists because they have temper problems or ... depression or anxiety, and it's really from a snowmobiling accident in [their] 30s."
Amen added that failing to protect the brain — which he described as "very soft" and having the consistency of "soft butter" — is "not the smart thing to do."
"Mild traumatic brain injury ruins people's lives," the brain expert said. (iStock)
Vision impairment
A significant portion of the brain is dedicated to vision, according to Amen.
"So, if your vision becomes troubled, your brain's troubled," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Amen said vision impairment may place additional demands on the brain. While the condition has been linked with cognitive decline, the WHO says there is insufficient evidence to recommend vision treatment specifically for dementia prevention.
Sleep disorders
Sleep appears to support the brain’s waste-clearance processes, Amen noted.
Sleep challenges affect tens of millions of Americans. In 2024, 30.5% of U.S. adults reported getting less than seven hours of shut-eye per day, according to the CDC.
For those with sleep problems such as sleep apnea, it can cause changes in the brain that resemble the hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease, the expert said.
Research suggests that sleep may help the brain clear beta-amyloid, although the relationship between sleep and dementia remains complex and is still being studied.
HIV
Inflammation and infections can affect brain health. Untreated HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) can affect the central nervous system and is associated with HIV-related cognitive impairment.
"If you love and care for your brain, you're going to love your life a whole bunch more."
Amen said he has scanned "hundreds of people" with HIV, stating that the virus is "clearly a risk factor."

Untreated HIV is known to affect the central nervous system and is associated with HIV-related cognitive impairment. Effective antiretroviral therapy has greatly reduced the incidence of severe HIV-associated dementia.
Air pollution
Exposure to any toxins, from alcohol and marijuana to lead, mercury or air pollution, could be detrimental to brain health, according to Amen.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The WHO recommends reducing exposure to household and outdoor air pollution, particularly fine particulate matter. Research has linked long-term exposure to air pollution with a higher risk of cognitive decline and dementia, although the WHO characterizes the evidence as low to very low certainty.
Exposure to any toxins, from alcohol and marijuana to lead, mercury or air pollution, is detrimental to brain health, the doctor warned. (iStock)
Getting ahead of it
Dementia risk rises sharply with age. A recent U.S. analysis estimated that about one in five people had developed dementia by age 85, with risk increasing further at older ages.
While those with a genetic predisposition to the disease have a higher risk, Amen noted that certain lifestyle factors can increase the risk for anyone.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"We should be on a dementia prevention program our whole lives," the doctor said. "It’s not something to start when you're 65."
Amen urged everyone to ask themselves the question: "Is what I’m doing good or bad for my brain?"
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Social activity is one of the prevention strategies. New learning is a prevention strategy," he added. "So always working on being connected with other people and then just making better decisions."
"If you love and care for your brain, you're going to love your life a whole bunch more."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Popular artificial sweetener linked to potentially dangerous heart risk
summary: A new study of over 17,700 participants links higher xylitol blood levels to increased cardiovascular risk, including heart attack and stroke, over future decades.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss a new study suggesting low sugar intake before age two leads to a reduced risk of developing dementia.
People who consume greater amounts of a popular artificial sweetener could face a greater risk of heart attack and stroke, a new study suggests.

The research, which was presented at the ESC Cardiology Congress in Germany this week, showed that higher levels of xylitol in the blood were associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).

Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that is commonly used as a low-calorie sweetener and sugar substitute, according to the National Institutes of Health. It is often used in higher amounts to sweeten foods, drinks, chewing gum and dental care products.
ZERO-CALORIE SWEETENERS COULD ALTER THE GENES OF LATER GENERATIONS, NEW STUDY WARNS
The researchers followed two large study cohorts of more than 17,700 Canadian and British participants.

Over a six-year follow-up, people in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging with the highest xylitol levels had a 57% higher risk of death, myocardial infarction or stroke related to cardiovascular events compared to those with the lowest levels.
People who consume greater amounts of a popular artificial sweetener could face a greater risk of heart attack and stroke, a new study suggests. (iStock)
Over 30 years, participants in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer (EPIC)-Norfolk group with the highest xylitol levels had an 18% greater risk of MACE.
Both cohorts showed evidence of a dose-dependent association, in which higher blood xylitol concentrations corresponded to higher rates of cardiovascular events.
DIRTY SODA DRINKS ARE EVERYWHERE, BUT DOCTORS WARN OF HEALTH RISKS: 'METABOLIC DISASTER'
These higher risks persisted even after the researchers adjusted for other factors like age, gender, body mass index, hypertension, diabetes and lipid levels.

The study follows previous research that showed xylitol can enhance the ability of platelets to form clots, according to Dr. Marco Witkowski, the study presenter from Charité University Hospital in Berlin, Germany.
Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that is commonly used as a low-calorie sweetener and sugar substitute. (iStock)
"Artificial sweeteners are consumed by people who think they are healthier than sugar, and they are generally regarded as safe by regulatory agencies," the doctor said in a statement.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Our long-term findings in the general population highlight how little we know about the cardiovascular safety of xylitol and indicate that further studies are warranted, especially as the amount of xylitol in products continues to increase."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The study was observational and does not prove that xylitol causes cardiovascular events, as the researchers noted that more studies are needed to confirm the findings.

The report also does not establish whether high levels of xylitol in the blood necessarily reflect dietary consumption, as the sugar alcohol can also be produced naturally in the body as part of glucose metabolism.
People with the highest xylitol levels had a 57% higher risk of death, myocardial infarction or stroke related to cardiovascular events compared to those with the lowest levels. (iStock)

"These disturbing findings with [a] plausible mechanism of xylitol increasing cardiovascular risk should be taken very seriously," Dr. Aseem Malhotra, a cardiologist and public health campaigner based in London, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"As a practicing cardiologist, I see many patients suffering from anxiety and palpitations that resolve as soon as they stop taking artificial sweeteners."
Malhotra, who was not involved in the study, noted that one of the most important dietary changes to reduce cardiovascular risk is to "unsweeten your sweet tooth."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"That’s why I advise all my patients to avoid all processed sugars and artificial sweeteners for six weeks to break the addiction," he added.
Fox News Digital reached out to several food and beverage trade groups for comment.

title: Dietitian reveals simple eating strategy for better sleep — and one habit to avoid
summary: Tart cherry juice tops a dietitian's list of sleep-boosting foods, with its natural melatonin content shown to improve both sleep quality and quantity.
story: The New Jersey-based registered dietitian and certified diabetes care specialist says certain foods can make, or break, a good night’s sleep, while a common habit can interfere with rest.
How you eat can influence how you sleep, according to experts.
Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based registered dietitian, certified diabetes care specialist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," says certain foods can make, or break, a good night’s sleep.
"There are a number of foods that can help support sleep, and sometimes it's even a combination," she told Fox News Digital.
5-STEP SLEEP RESET COULD PROMOTE HEALTHY WEIGHT LOSS, NUTRITIONIST SAYS
Supporting better sleep
Keeping blood sugar steady throughout the day may help prevent afternoon energy crashes and support more restorative sleep at night, Palinski-Wade said.
Waking up in the middle of the night and struggling to fall back asleep may not always be insomnia, she suggested, but could be linked to fluctuations in glucose levels.
Keeping blood sugar steady throughout the day may help prevent afternoon energy crashes and support more restorative sleep at night. (iStock)
Combining lean proteins, slow-digesting carbohydrates and healthy fats in meals and snacks can help stabilize those levels — what Palinski-Wade called the "No. 1 way" to improve overall sleep.
Some small studies suggest tart cherry juice may support sleep, and the expert named tart cherries — or 100% tart cherry juice — as her top choice.
FOOD CRAVINGS AT 3:45 PM AREN'T RANDOM, HERE'S WHAT YOUR BODY MAY BE WARNING YOU ABOUT

"Tart cherries [are] one of the foods that have the highest amount of melatonin naturally, but they also have compounds that help to really extend that melatonin in our bodies and our body's ability to use it," she said.
Still, research linking tart cherry consumption to modest improvements in sleep duration or quality is limited and mixed; a 2025 systematic review reached a similar conclusion.
The expert recommends ingesting 4 to 6 ounces of 100% tart cherry juice or about a quarter cup of dried tart cherries for better sleep. (iStock)
For those who suffer from insomnia, Palinski-Wade recommends ingesting 4 to 6 ounces of 100% tart cherry juice, or about a quarter cup of dried tart cherries.
"It's a really, really great tool to improve your sleep – and it's really tasty, too," she said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Foods and drinks that may help reduce inflammation can also support sleep, the dietitian said.
"When we have more antioxidants in the body, more anti-inflammatory compounds, we're really helping our body to achieve that more restful state," Palinski-Wade said.
Foods rich in antioxidants and anti-inflammatory compounds — including nuts and seeds, olive oil and avocados — also provide healthy fats and other nutrients that may support sleep.
Any more than 300 milligrams of caffeine per day becomes a "stressor to our body," the expert warned. (iStock)
Caffeine’s sleep impact
On the other hand, Palinski-Wade warned that caffeine intake can negatively impact sleep quality.

"So many of us have a poor night's sleep and the next day we reach for caffeine to give us a burst of energy," she said. "And there's nothing wrong with a little bit of caffeine, but you have to look at how much you're having and how close to bedtime."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"And it's a stimulant, so it's harder to fall asleep," Palinski-Wade warned. "If you have foods or beverages with a large amount of caffeine, and you're having them in the afternoon or toward the evening, that is going to make it very hard to get restorative, restful sleep in the evening."
For those who do drink caffeine, it is best to stop about 10 hours before bedtime, the expert advised.
Stimulation and inflammation from caffeine can disrupt sleep if consumed too close to bedtime. (iStock)
The "sweet spot" for daily caffeine intake is 300 milligrams or less, she said. Any more than that becomes a "stressor to our body." A cup of coffee, traditionally 8 ounces, is about 100 milligrams.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The FDA says up to 400 milligrams daily is not generally associated with negative effects for most adults, although individual tolerance can vary depending on factors such as medications, health conditions and sensitivity to caffeine.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We start to release stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, and that not only makes our body store fat versus burn it, but it also increases inflammation," Palinski-Wade noted.
"So now you have the stimulant, you have this inflammation, and all those things go against quality sleep."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Why Dolly Parton’s death can feel like losing someone you knew personally
summary: Fans worldwide describe "post-Parton depression" as Dolly Parton's death triggers intense parasocial grief that psychologists say mirrors real loss.
story: Dolly Parton, the Grammy-winning singer, songwriter and philanthropist whose career spanned over six decades, has died at 80.
The death of Dolly Parton has prompted an outpouring of grief from fans around the world, many of whom have shared that they feel like they’ve lost someone they knew personally.

Grief experts say it’s possible to experience genuine feelings of loss even if there wasn’t a personal relationship — particularly when the public figure has become woven into people’s memories and routines over a long period of time.
Psychologists refer to this type of loss as parasocial grief, according to licensed clinical psychologist Dr. Dara Houp.
DOLLY PARTON’S PRIVATE CANCER BATTLE HIGHLIGHTS WHY SOME PATIENTS DON’T SHARE THEIR DIAGNOSES

"When a celebrity shares their personal life – childhood experiences, hardships and victories – our brains register these bits of information through the same emotional and neural pathways utilized for our real-life friendships and a genuine attachment is developed," Houp, with Pathways Psychological Services in New York City, told Fox News Digital.
When that perceived relationship comes to an end, people may experience the parasocial grief, she said.

\Fans of Dolly Parton visit a mural featuring her likeness in the city's North Side on Aug. 26, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. Fans across the nation are mourning the death of the country music star, actress and philanthropist who died on Tuesday at age 80. (Getty Images)

Desiree Taranto, a licensed mental health counselor and clinical director at Empower Your Mind Therapy in New York City, said the widespread reaction also reflects "collective grief," a shared emotional response when a loss resonates across a community.
"Parton’s music, movies, philanthropy and public persona became part of many people’s family traditions, memories and difficult life moments," she told Fox News Digital.
Fans share their grief

"I honestly didn’t know I could react that way over someone I don’t even personally know," one user wrote in a grief support group on Reddit. "[Dolly] was a ray of sunshine in this dark world nowadays, and I just can’t help but cry and get so emotional about it."
Another user shared that "as each day passes, losing Dolly seems to hurt more instead of less. I have found myself crying and feeling this deep sadness that I just can’t shake."
IN WAKE OF DOLLY PARTON'S DEATH, ONCOLOGIST REVEALS WHY SOME PATIENTS KEEP CANCER DIAGNOSES SECRET
"I never met Dolly, and I know she didn’t know me, but I loved her for most of my life. That love was real, and so this grief feels real too."
Someone else in a different group referred to the feelings of sadness as "post-Parton depression."
Fans honor Dolly Parton with flowers, notes and small gifts at the site of her star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Aug. 26, 2026 in Hollywood, California. (Getty Images)
"I don't know why I am taking Dolly Parton's death so hard," one user wrote. "I never met her… She didn't know me. But for some reason, I can't stop crying."
"I think the reason it's hard is because she was a light and just a wonderful human," someone else shared. "She is exactly who Jesus wanted us to be."
Why does it feel personal?
The emotions people experience when grieving a celebrity can feel as real as those felt after losing someone they knew personally, Houp said.

"Perceived relational intimacy, not whether we actually know an individual, is largely what determines the intensity of grief," she said. "The emotional connection your brain developed runs along the same neural pathways as real-life bonds."
"Accept your feelings and know that it is okay to mourn someone you never met."

It’s also possible that the deaths of certain celebrities — particularly those associated with childhood, family traditions or major life moments — are more likely to trigger an intense grief response, the expert noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"When a celebrity’s life is connected to a personal milestone — such as a break-up or the birth of a child — their death permanently disrupts a living connection to who, what or where you used to be," Houp said. "Losing a celebrity can feel like losing a piece of your own history."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A song may be tied to someone who has died, a family memory or a difficult period when Parton’s work brought comfort, Taranto noted, making the loss feel connected to a person’s own life story.
Over decades in the public eye, Parton gave fans a window into her life, allowing them to form a sense of who she was, Houp said.
Fans pay tribute to Dolly Parton at her home in Brentwood on Aug. 25, 2026 in Brentwood, Tennessee. (Getty Images)
"For many who followed Dolly’s life, she represented resilience and ambition, authenticity and bold self-expression, and a rare, unconditional kindness," she said.
"We identified with the goodness we saw in Dolly and felt encouraged by her ability to overcome hardship – thereby furthering our sense of connection to her."
Tips to navigate grief
Taranto offered advice for those feeling the grief following Parton’s death.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Accept your feelings and know that it is okay to mourn someone you never met," she said. "Do not judge yourself or feel embarrassed because that person’s work, values or advocacy touched your life personally."
It can also help to reach out to others who are also grieving the loss.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Be there for each other and allow others to be there for you," Taranto advised. "Tell stories, listen to her music, watch her movies or journal about what she meant to you."
"Remember the positive impact she made in the world and the ways she used her platform for good. Shared grief can help us process a loss because it reminds us that we are not alone in it."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Drug institute warns that Trump-shaped ecstasy pills contain potentially fatal ingredient
summary: The Trimbos Institute in the Netherlands issued a red alert after Donald Trump-shaped ecstasy pills containing potentially fatal PMMA were handed in at testing centers.
story: President Donald Trump highlighted a massive drop in fentanyl deaths and illegal drugs entering the country by sea in an exclusive interview with Trace Gallagher.
A respected drug treatment and mental health center in the Netherlands issued a warning against taking ecstasy pills shaped like President Donald Trump’s head, saying they could be fatal.

The Trimbos Institute warned in a "red alert" that the pills contain a high concentration of PMMA, also known as para-methoxymethamphetamine, which is similar to ecstasy’s active ingredient MDMA but is slower acting.
The slow onset could encourage users to take more and potentially overdose.
The institute shared a photo of two of the pills, one of which was green on the front and the other yellow. They were red and blue on the back.
POLICE SEIZE COCAINE BRICKS WITH STICKERS OF NORWEGIAN SOCCER STAR ERLING HAALAND ALL OVER THEM

This undated photo provided by the Trimbos Institute of Mental Health and Addiction shows pills with a depiction of President Donald Trump on one side and NL and Trump stamped on the other. (Trimbos Institute of Mental Health and Addiction via AP)
The pills had a likeness of Trump’s face on the front and the name "Trump" and letters "NL" on the back.
"Absolutely do not use these pills," the institute said.
In 2018, Indiana State police seized orange Trump-shaped ecstasy pills in an operation targeting small-time drug traffickers.
Those pills also had Trump’s face on the front and "great again" written on the back, an apparent reference to his Make America Great Again slogan.
The institute said the pills have a slow-acting ingredient that could lead to overdose. (Trimbos Institute of Mental Health and Addiction via AP)
In 2017, German police also seized thousands of Trump-shaped ecstasy pills, which also appeared to be orange, that had an estimated street value of nearly $46,000.
There have yet to be any reports of overdoses or deaths due to the drug, spokesperson Anniek Groothuis told The Associated Press.
GERMAN POLICE SEIZE THOUSANDS OF 'TRUMP' ECSTASY TABLETS
"We do not know of any victims where PMMA was found in their blood," she said.
Indiana State Police released a photo showing ecstasy pills bearing President Trump's image and the words "great again" in 2018. (Indiana State Police )
The clinic said the pills had recently been handed in to some of its centers where it tests drugs before people take them.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, hundreds of thousands of people use the drug every year, according to the government.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Quiet quitting’ in marriage: The subtle signs a spouse has emotionally checked out
summary: Licensed therapist Lisa Brookes Kift outlines how "quiet quitting" erodes marriages and why the absence of arguing may signal emotional detachment.
story: Dr. Anna Elton discusses why stressed partners may lose interest in physical affection and how regular check-ins, gratitude and intentional time together can change the dynamic at home.
"Quiet quitting," a workplace term for doing only the minimum required, has also been used to describe a pattern in some marriages.
In relationships, the informal term refers to spouses who remain together while reducing their emotional effort, communication or involvement in the relationship.
Couples may continue managing day-to-day responsibilities, such as household tasks and parenting, even as one partner becomes emotionally and physically disengaged, relationship experts say.
‘NO CONTACT’ ON THE RISE: NEARLY 2 IN 5 AMERICANS CUT TIES WITH LOVED ONES
Discussion of the term has gained traction on social media, with users sharing videos and posts about remaining in a marriage while feeling checked out.
Licensed marriage and family therapist Lisa Brookes Kift of Marin Therapy and Counseling in California told Fox News Digital that a noticeable absence of friction can be an early warning sign.
A couple lying in bed and looking at their cellular phones, ignoring each other (iStock)

"It’s a myth that an absence of arguing in a relationship automatically means the relationship is healthy," Kift said. "Many are conflict-avoidant and rather than address their feelings, opt to sweep them under the rug, which over the long term erodes the foundation of emotional safety."
Kift said a person’s attachment style — patterns of seeking closeness and support in relationships — can influence how they respond to marital distress.
CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT
"An avoidant style may be more able to stay in their own lane — on their own island — to ride it out, because they are most comfortable resourcing in themselves," she said.

Those with a more secure attachment style are less likely to stay in that dynamic because they may be more inclined to give a partner the benefit of the doubt and believe problems can be worked through, the expert noted.
Early lessons about trust, worthiness and whether personal needs will be met heavily influence how a partner handles marital distress. (bymuratdeniz via Getty Images)
These patterns can be shaped, in part, by early experiences involving trust, worthiness and whether a person’s emotional needs were met, according to Kift.
"What did they learn about whether their needs would be met? Whether the most important people to them could be trusted? That they were lovable for who they were and not what they did?" Kift asked.
When adult relationships appear to repeat those early disappointments, partners can lose hope, she added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"I’ve seen quite a few people in my therapy practice who have taken this stance, where there have been failed attempts to get emotional and other needs met, leading to hopelessness," Kift said.
Kift identified several early signs that a partner may be becoming emotionally disengaged.
