title: DOJ asks Supreme Court to allow Trump’s USPS action on mail-in ballots to proceed ahead of midterm elections
summary: The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to green-light a new Postal Service rule that would exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections.
story: The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to green-light a new Postal Service rule that would exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections.
The appeal to the high court comes after U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani last week issued a temporary restraining order blocking parts of the rule from being implemented.

“With respect to the November 2026 election, the order thus partially nullifies the Postal Service’s efforts to address the risk that the federal mails will be used to perpetrate voter fraud, a particularly pernicious species of fraud that dilutes the votes of lawful voters, prevents election results from reflecting the will of the American people, and undermines ‘public confidence in the integrity of the electoral process,’” Solicitor General John Sauer wrote in the application.

While Talwani’s order “allows the Postal Service and the States to continue taking steps to ensure that their envelopes satisfy the rule’s requirements, the order risks sowing confusion and chaos because it makes those preparatory steps voluntary, rather than mandatory,” Sauer wrote.

There is a “grave risk,” Sauer writes, “that States may not have taken the necessary steps to comply due to the false sense of latitude created by the court’s improper order, potentially depriving those States’ citizens of the ability to vote by mail.”
It seeks an immediate stay of Talwani’s order while the case proceeds through the appeals court.

The timing of the request was unexpected, since the administration already had a pending appeal of the order to the First U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, and because Talwani was expected to rule Thursday on whether to issue a preliminary injunction in the case.

In her ruling last week, the judge sided with states and voting rights groups that claimed the rule unlawfully usurped states’ power to regulate their own elections, which is something that would need congressional approval, and left them facing an “impossible” timeline to comply in time for the November elections.

“Through the Final Rule, the USPS is refusing to send mail ballots to eligible voters unless States or local election officials submit their mail ballot envelopes and return envelopes and receive advance approval from the USPS without regard to impending deadlines for the November 3, 2026 election,” the judge wrote.

It also “requires elections officials to create accounts for a new electronic portal, certify that they have received approval regarding the mail ballot design, and thereafter upload to the USPS portal each voter’s information, including name, address, and a unique intelligent mail barcode,” she noted.

“Based on the record presently before the court, Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible as to the 2026 midterm elections, now little more than two months away,” Talwani wrote.

She said most states have already ordered their mail ballots “and some are required by state law to send them to eligible voters as early as next week.” North Carolina is scheduled to begin mailing out ballots Friday.

The states, she added, “have neither time nor funds to design new mail ballots, seek approval of the new designs, order production of mail ballots, update their own election management systems, train election officials to use the USPS portal, and upload citizen data to the portal, all before the midterms.”
While the government has said the measure is necessary to combat voter fraud, Talwani said it had not presented “any evidence regarding fraudulent absentee or mail-in voting.”

The “USPS’s interest in correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement of citizens who need access to mail ballots in order to vote,” she wrote.
The rule change came about as the result of an executive order issued by President Donald Trump on March 31 titled “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections.”

Talwani had signed off on an earlier order in a related case barring the rule from being implemented, but that ruling was overturned last month by the Supreme Court, which found her decision was premature because the rule had not yet been finalized.

“The court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the court said in an unsigned 6-3 ruling.
The rule was finalized late last month.
In court filings, the government said the changes that are being implemented are “modest.”

The rule simply turns “longstanding recommendations—which many of the Plaintiff States have already adopted at least in part, and some have long advocated for—into requirements,” the government argued.

It added that “this is ultimately a regulation of the U.S. mail, and a modest one at that—not a federal takeover of election administration by the Postal Service. That basic reality undermines virtually all of Plaintiffs’ claims and illustrates why Defendants are likely to succeed on the merits of their appeal.”

title: Missouri Supreme Court rules new GOP-drawn map can’t be used for November elections
summary: The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the state’s redrawn congressional map cannot be used in this year’s midterm elections, dealing a major blow to Republicans.
story: The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the state’s redrawn congressional map cannot be used in this year’s midterm elections, dealing a blow to Republicans.

The court ruled that a referendum that will determine whether the state can use the map going forward must appear on the November ballot, meaning Missouri’s fall elections will take place under its previous district lines.
The new map was designed to draw one of the two Missouri Democrats in Congress, longtime Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, out of his seat.
The ruling comes after a protracted battle between advocacy group People Not Politicians Missouri, who sought to block the Republican redistricting effort, and the state GOP leaders who defended it.

Missouri redrew its congressional map in 2025 at the behest of President Donald Trump. In response, People Not Politicians Missouri gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force a veto referendum. And while the group exceeded the signature requirements for getting on the ballot, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins refused to certify it, saying that it was unconstitutional. The group appealed to the state Supreme Court, who heard arguments on the matter on Wednesday.
The ruling comes just days before the state’s Sept. 8 deadline to finalize its ballot for the general election. The state ran its August primary election using the Republican-drawn map.

Judge Ginger K. Gooch wrote in her ruling that Hoskins and those acting with him “are restrained and enjoined from implementing, using, or mandating the use of the congressional redistricting in HB 1 for the November 2026 general election or at any other time thereafter unless and until HB 1 is approved by the voters at the November 2026 general election and takes effect 30 days thereafter.”
The court’s decision means Cleaver will now be seeking re-election for his old seat, which skews heavily Democratic. He won by almost 24 percentage points in 2024.
The redesigned 5th District, which was struck down by Thursday’s ruling, was drawn so that Trump would have won by more than 17 points in 2024.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway vowed in a statement following the ruling to appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court.

“Never before in American history has a court overturned a congressional map after a primary and before a general election. This unprecedented decision clearly violates federal law and has thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis,” Hanaway wrote. “We are confident that the federal courts will not allow every Missouri voter to be disenfranchised—which is what today’s decision does.”
People Not Politicians executive director Richard von Glahn celebrated the ruling.

“This victory reaches beyond Missouri. In a year when map-drawing has become a national weapon, courts across the country are watching what happens here. A Missouri win for the referendum is a signal that the people still hold the power,” Glahn said in a statement.
Missouri is one of a handful of Republican-led states that took up mid-decade redistricting efforts at Trump’s urging to shore up the party’s narrow House majority.

title: Feds charge ICE officer with lying to investigators in the shooting of Venezuelan immigrant
summary: A federal grand jury returned an indictment against Christian Castro in the January shooting that left Julio Cesar Sosa Celis with a gunshot wound in one of his legs.
story: An ICE officer is facing federal charges for allegedly lying to federal investigators about the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant during immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis earlier this year.

A federal grand jury on Wednesday returned an indictment charging the officer, Christian Castro, with making false statements to the FBI about the Jan. 14 shooting that left Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis with a gunshot wound in his leg, a source familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
A separate investigation into whether Castro should face a more serious civil rights charge in the shooting is ongoing, the source added.
The Associated Press first reported on Castro’s latest federal charges.

The federal charges come a week after Castro was released from jail in Texas despite an extradition warrant from Minnesota prosecutors seeking his transfer. He’s facing state charges in Minnesota accusing him of assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.

Federal authorities had initially accused Sosa-Celis and another man of beating an immigration officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel in a confrontation that preceded the shooting, but federal prosecutors dropped the charges they filed against the men after video evidence showed the ICE officers may have lied about the encounter.

Castro was arrested in May in the Minnesota case. He was held in custody in Brownsville, Texas, until his release last week after a judge and Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign his extradition warrant — citing fraud investigations involving social services programs in Minnesota, which the Trump administration used to justify his immigration crackdown there.
Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary, told NBC News that “state law enforcement stands ready and willing to assist federal partners in facilitating Mr. Castro’s arrest if needed.”
Mahaleris added that “details of any federal indictment are best addressed to the U.S. Department of Justice.”
The Department of Homeland Security and the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office referred any queries to the DOJ.
An attorney for Castro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As news broke of Castro’s latest indictment, a federal prosecutor working on the case against Castro was fired, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Evans had told lawyers for Sosa-Celis that DOJ officials have blocked efforts to bring the more serious civil rights charge against Castro, ProPublica reported on Wednesday.
Evans did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and his DOJ email address returned an automated reply saying he was on leave.

title: OpenAI releases new model that it says triggered internal security measures
summary: The AI giant says its model better follows user intent and crosses a frontier for cybersecurity capabilities, and could be artificial general intelligence.
story: OpenAI released its newest and most powerful model, called GPT-6 Astra, Thursday to a limited set of customers, labelling it the world’s most intelligent AI system and the first model to trigger advanced internal safety protections given its cyber capabilities.

The company said the model sets a new high-water mark for its ability to autonomously control computer systems and perform tasks on behalf of users, such as filling out spreadsheets and  creating websites from scratch.
“Astra can really do anything a human can do with a computer,” OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said before the model was released.

Brockman said that Astra represented a “jump” in capabilities for its AI systems and said it would be reasonable to see Astra as a version of artificial general intelligence (AGI), often referred to as AI systems that can perform most meaningful tasks as well as humans. “Welcome to the AGI era!” Brockman said.

The company also emphasized that the model is faster and more efficient than its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol, on a variety of tasks. For example, OpenAI said that Astra achieved a higher score using fewer output tokens, a common unit of measurement for AI tasks, on a key cybersecurity test called ExploitGym.
“Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browser use, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing Astra’s release.

OpenAI said Astra would first be made available to participants in its Daybreak program for cybersecurity defenders, with wider access for enterprise and consumer accounts planned for the coming days.

Astra’s release comes just days after rival Anthropic released its latest models, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, which it said set its own new frontiers for a range of scientific, coding and reasoning tasks.

Both companies said their respective models were world-leading AI systems. OpenAI called Astra “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model.” Rival Anthropic crowned its own systems as “the world’s most advanced models for coding and knowledge work.”
Astra’s release comes amid rising concerns and scrutiny about frontier AI companies’ cybersecurity protocols and ability to control their own technology.

In a report released last week, OpenAI said that a model in the same family as Astra that was not meant for public release managed to autonomously establish administrator control over part of OpenAI’s own infrastructure and potentially exposed secret OpenAI information to the open internet.
The company said this activity, along with other “misaligned” behavior, happened without the knowledge of its staff members, despite some internal efforts to monitor AI agents.
“As these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” said Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, on Thursday.

On Tuesday, OpenAI said that Astra was its first model to cross certain internal capability thresholds for implementing stricter security measures, as laid out in its longstanding Preparedness Framework.

Astra “can find previously unknown security flaws and develop ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step,” the company wrote in a Tuesday blog post. OpenAI said it rolled out increased cybersecurity protocols over the past several weeks.
The company said Astra will feature increased monitoring mechanisms, so OpenAI can “rapidly detect and contain potentially misaligned actions.”
However, Pachocki said that current techniques for monitoring and observing models’ behavior may not hold, as AI systems become more advanced and potentially evade human monitors’ oversight.
He said the company takes this loss of oversight and insight seriously, and that it would factor into its future development decisions.
“We will not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We will withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence,” he said.

On Tuesday, The Information reported that a training technique involved in Astra’s development could drastically decrease humans’ ability to understand how the AI system “thinks” or processes user commands.
The report triggered a firestorm of online criticism about decreased safety protocols. Pachocki pushed back on that reporting, writing on X that he wanted “to prevent a race into unmonitorability.”

Despite growing challenges in overseeing AI systems’ behavior, OpenAI also said that Astra better follows and understands user intent, while less frequently trying to cheat or work around internal protections compared to GPT-5.6 Sol.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that Astra also went through the White House’s voluntary vetting process for cutting-edge AI systems, telling Axios on Wednesday that “of course” the company decided to let the administration review Astra.

Brockman said the White House did not request any substantial changes to Astra. “There is nothing that they came back with saying that you need to change this in terms of safeguards,” he said Thursday.

Many AI experts and members of Congress are clamoring for more visibility into the exact way the White House and federal offices involved with AI, including the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and the National Security Agency, test advanced AI systems before they are released to the public.

title: Fox News parts ways with Maria Bartiromo
summary: Fox News has parted ways with longtime anchor Maria Bartiromo, a vocal defender of President Donald Trump who hosted several financial news shows.
story: Fox News said Thursday that it had parted ways with longtime anchor Maria Bartiromo, a vocal defender of President Donald Trump who hosted several financial news shows.
“We thank Maria for her work over the lasts 12½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter,” a spokesperson said in a statement that did not elaborate further.

Bartiromo has been Fox Business Network’s global markets editor since joining it in 2014. She hosted “Mornings with Maria” and “Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street” on Fox Business, while also anchoring “Sunday Morning Futures,” a business-focused show on Fox News Channel.
Bartiromo joined Fox from CNBC, where she hosted one of the network’s highest-profile programs, “Closing Bell” and was the first person to report live from the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.
Bartiromo’s departure was “effective today,” said the Fox spokesperson.

Bartiromo built a reputation as a trailblazer for women in financial media and television broadcasting. She drew attention in media circles for taking a more openly conservative turn in her reporting after leaving CNBC, where her work had been largely apolitical.
Many of Trump’s Cabinet secretaries appeared regularly on her shows during both of his terms in office. Fox also regularly touted Bartiromo’s shows as ratings winners.

In 2021, Bartiromo’s comments and shows were cited as exhibits in a defamation lawsuit filed by the voting machine maker Dominion Voting Systems against Fox News. Dominion alleged that the cable network operator had knowingly broadcast false claimed that Dominion had rigged the 2020 presidential election.
Fox News and Dominion eventually settled the lawsuit in 2023 for $787 million.
During her nearly 21 years at CNBC, Bartiromo appeared regularly on national broadcast programs, including NBC’s “TODAY” and “Nightly News” during the 2007-2008 financial crisis.
Comcast, the parent company of NBC News, spun off CNBC in 2025.
Bartiromo did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on her departure.
Bartiromo has not appeared on FBN’s air since Aug. 9, according to a review of archived episodes of her shows. Her biography page and show pages had already been removed from Fox’s websites Thursday.
Bartiromo was one of the first financial journalists on cable TV whose influence extended beyond Wall Street.
Early in her career, Bartiromo had been dubbed the “Money Honey,” a nickname she later said she had misgivings about.
In the early 1990s, The Ramones’ Joey Ramone released a song titled “Maria Bartiromo.”
She also appeared in the 2010 film “Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps,” where she played herself alongside Michael Douglas’ Gordon Gekko in a scene set at a fictional CNBC interview.

title: In Nepal, mourners hold symbolic cremation for missing loved ones
summary: The wall of ice, water and rock that tore through Nepal last week has claimed more than 1,200 lives and left more than 4,000 missing, depriving many grieving families of a basic rite: funerals.
story: The wall of ice, water and rock that tore through Nepal last week has claimed more than 1,200 lives and left more than 4,000 missing, depriving many grieving families of a basic rite: funerals.

The scale of the disaster has proved challenging for authorities, with morgues overwhelmed by a large number of unidentified remains. In many cases, bodies have been washed far downstream and rendered unrecognizable, while others still missing are feared to have been buried in the torrent of thick mud.
As hopes fade that survivors will be found, a week on from the disaster, family members without the remains of their loved ones have begun to hold symbolic cremations.
The ceremonies provide an outlet for the grief and uncertainty that have gripped so many in Nepal, and ensure that a key religious rite is afforded to the dead.

At Kathmandu’s Pashupatinath Temple, the most revered Hindu temple in Nepal, mourners gathered Wednesday to mark the loss of missing loved ones. On the banks of the holy Bagmati River, they burned effigies made of kusa grass, also called darbha, a plant used in Hindu rituals, on miniature funeral pyres.
The small stick figures, wrapped in orange cloth, were rubbed in paste and covered in garlands of orange flowers.

title: Colin Kaepernick is done with the NFL. He isn’t done fighting.
summary: Ten years after taking a knee to stand against racism and police brutality at great cost to his career and finances, Colin Kaepernick is back in the spotlight.
story: Colin Kaepernick still puts in a workout at 4:30 a.m. most days. His football life may be long over, but his life’s work is not.
Ten years after taking a knee to stand against racism and police brutality at great cost to his career and finances, the former star quarterback is stepping back into the spotlight.
Add to Google
Add to Google

His memoir, “The Perilous Fight,” comes out on Sept. 15. And in interviews with NBC News, his first time speaking in depth about his protest’s fallout in years, Kaepernick reveals the story behind how he came to take a knee in 2016, an act that made him both a hero and a pariah, and one of the most divisive figures in the country.

Kaepernick, 38, is now also a father of a 4-year-old girl. That, he says, helped him understand he has unfinished business in his life and cause. Being a dad “increases the responsibility and urgency of the work we’re doing,” he says. He doesn’t want his daughter — or anyone else — to think he stopped fighting or that the fight was not worth it.  “I don’t want my community to watch me and have the takeaway be that if you fight for Black folks, it’s over for you,” he writes in his book.
More NBC News coverage of Colin Kaepernick

Kaepernick will be the first guest on "Before & After with Lester Holt," available as soon as Sept. 7.Kaepernick is set to appear on "TODAY" on Sept. 16.Read Kaepernick's response to Jay-Z's recent freestyle rap about him on NBC News on Wednesday.
Kaepernick will be the first guest on "Before & After with Lester Holt," available as soon as Sept. 7.
Kaepernick is set to appear on "TODAY" on Sept. 16.
Read Kaepernick's response to Jay-Z's recent freestyle rap about him on NBC News on Wednesday.

Much has shifted in American politics, culture, sports and policing since 2016. And much work still needs to be done, Kaepernick says, which is why he chose now to recount the decade-long odyssey that began with a quiet protest during the national anthem.

Though the years have provided perspective, Kaepernick says they haven’t dulled his displeasure with the NFL. The quarterback who once led the San Francisco 49ers on a Disney movie-esque run to the Super Bowl in 2012 says he hasn’t watched an NFL game since he was exiled from the league.

“I’m not gonna support an organization that one, is actively blackballing me, but two, has targeted my brothers who have been protesting as part of this as well,” Kaepernick says. “I watch college football.”
(NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has said on multiple occasions he doesn’t believe Kaepernick was blackballed.)

On Sept. 1, 2016, Kaepernick and his San Francisco 49ers teammate Eric Reid kneeled during the national anthem before a preseason game. It was not the first time Kaepernick didn’t stand. His protest actually began a month earlier, on Aug. 14, when he sat on the bench during “The Star-Spangled Banner.”
The idea had simmered in the months prior to the season when, he writes in his memoir, he was recuperating from surgeries. He might not have taken a knee if he hadn’t injured it first.

The rehab gave him more free time than he ever had in his life. And in the midst of news of police violence, Kaepernick immersed himself in literature on Black liberation, reading books such as “The Autobiography of Malcolm X” and “Black Skin, White Masks” by Frantz Fanon.

title: California woman who served a decade in prison for killing a partner will now serve 36 more for murdering her wife
summary: The California woman who fled to Mexico after fatally stabbing her wife, a captain with the state’s wildland firefighting agency, was sentenced this week to 36 years to life in prison, officials said.
story: The California woman who fled to Mexico after fatally stabbing her wife, a captain with the state’s wildland firefighting agency, was sentenced this week to 36 years to life in prison, officials said.

Yolanda Marodi, 54, pleaded guilty last month to second-degree murder in the Feb. 17, 2025, death of Rebecca Marodi, 49, at the couple’s home in Ramona, northeast of San Diego, the county’s district attorney said in a statement.
Yolanda Marodi previously pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter in the death of an estranged partner in 2003 and served roughly a decade in prison.
Yolanda and Rebecca Marodi’s marriage of roughly two years was deteriorating when Yolanda Marodi stabbed her wife roughly two dozen times, the district attorney’s office said.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Some of the events of Feb. 17, 2025, were captured in grim security camera video from the couple’s patio, according to an affidavit in support of an arrest warrant. When a bloodied Rebecca Marodi told her wife that she didn’t want to die, Yolanda Marodi responded, “You should have thought about that before.”
Roughly a week earlier, the affidavit states, Rebecca Marodi had told her wife she planned on ending their marriage.
In a text message cited in the affidavit, Yolanda Marodi told someone that she hurt Rebecca Marodi after learning that the relationship was over and her wife said she’d met someone else.
Yolanda Marodi was captured in Mexicali, just south of the U.S. border, on March 22, 2025.
During Wednesday’s sentencing hearing, Rebecca Marodi’s mother said it had been “the privilege of a lifetime” to be her parent.
“In the face of the greatest darkness, I have stood strong to receive justice for my amazing, beautiful, strong daughter,” said Lorena Marodi, who found her daughter’s body and called 911.

“Every morning when I wake, the image of my baby girl lying on the floor with stab wounds to her back and lifeless haunts me,” she said. “Despite the horrific violence bestowed upon Becky, I refuse to allow Yolanda’s darkness to consume me.”

title: Missouri Supreme Court rules new GOP-drawn map can’t be used for November elections
summary: The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the state’s redrawn congressional map cannot be used in this year’s midterm elections, dealing a major blow to Republicans.
story: The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the state’s redrawn congressional map cannot be used in this year’s midterm elections, dealing a blow to Republicans.

The court ruled that a referendum that will determine whether the state can use the map going forward must appear on the November ballot, meaning Missouri’s fall elections will take place under its previous district lines.
The new map was designed to draw one of the two Missouri Democrats in Congress, longtime Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, out of his seat.
The ruling comes after a protracted battle between advocacy group People Not Politicians Missouri, who sought to block the Republican redistricting effort, and the state GOP leaders who defended it.

Missouri redrew its congressional map in 2025 at the behest of President Donald Trump. In response, People Not Politicians Missouri gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force a veto referendum. And while the group exceeded the signature requirements for getting on the ballot, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins refused to certify it, saying that it was unconstitutional. The group appealed to the state Supreme Court, who heard arguments on the matter on Wednesday.
The ruling comes just days before the state’s Sept. 8 deadline to finalize its ballot for the general election. The state ran its August primary election using the Republican-drawn map.

Judge Ginger K. Gooch wrote in her ruling that Hoskins and those acting with him “are restrained and enjoined from implementing, using, or mandating the use of the congressional redistricting in HB 1 for the November 2026 general election or at any other time thereafter unless and until HB 1 is approved by the voters at the November 2026 general election and takes effect 30 days thereafter.”
The court’s decision means Cleaver will now be seeking re-election for his old seat, which skews heavily Democratic. He won by almost 24 percentage points in 2024.
The redesigned 5th District, which was struck down by Thursday’s ruling, was drawn so that Trump would have won by more than 17 points in 2024.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway vowed in a statement following the ruling to appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court.

“Never before in American history has a court overturned a congressional map after a primary and before a general election. This unprecedented decision clearly violates federal law and has thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis,” Hanaway wrote. “We are confident that the federal courts will not allow every Missouri voter to be disenfranchised—which is what today’s decision does.”
People Not Politicians executive director Richard von Glahn celebrated the ruling.

“This victory reaches beyond Missouri. In a year when map-drawing has become a national weapon, courts across the country are watching what happens here. A Missouri win for the referendum is a signal that the people still hold the power,” Glahn said in a statement.
Missouri is one of a handful of Republican-led states that took up mid-decade redistricting efforts at Trump’s urging to shore up the party’s narrow House majority.

title: How Trump is leaving his mark – literally – on Washington and beyond: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Andrea Mitchell reviews the ways President Donald Trump is leaving a physical stamp on the nation’s capital. Plus, we dig into the Cabinet officials Republicans want on the stump this fall.
Programming note: We’re off tomorrow ahead of the holiday weekend. We’ll be back in your inbox on Tuesday.
— Adam Wollner
Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.
How Trump is leaving his mark — literally — on Washington and beyond
President Donald Trump often describes himself as a builder.

Last week, he showed off the new helipad covering a large swath of the South Lawn to visiting schoolchildren. He frequently displays renderings of his proposed arch and ballroom in the Oval Office. And during a meeting with oil industry executives earlier this year, he extolled the ballroom excavation that could be seen outside an East Room window, which the Supreme Court has allowed to proceed.

There is no question that Trump is reshaping national parks, memorials and the physical landscape of the nation’s capital. Today, a federal judge blessed the administration’s plans to replace a popular, inexpensive public golf course with what he has called a “world class championship” course modeled after his own. With construction scheduled for this month, bicyclists and preservationists opposed the administration chopping down 150 trees, including Japanese cherry trees. The Justice Department told a court today that 77 of the cut-down trees were determined to be “invasive” and 73 were taken down because they were “dead, dying or hazardous.”

Judge Ana Reyes said she found “no reason” not to believe the government but remarked it was ironic that 250 years after the nation’s birth, “we are here talking about a president yet again chopping down cherry trees.”

There are other ways that Trump is leaving his mark on Washington. Banners with his image have appeared on government buildings, including the traditionally independent Department of Justice. His portrait is now also on a $1 golden coin commemorating the country’s 250 birthday.

Known in the real estate business for branding his buildings, Trump added his name to the U.S. Institute of Peace, a privately funded nonprofit think tank across from the State Department, days before a challenge to his takeover was to be heard in court. In another case, a federal judge ordered Trump’s name removed from the Kennedy Center façade because the 1964 legislation that created the center designated it as Washington’s sole memorial to President John F. Kennedy, barring any renaming. The White House is appealing but went on to name the surrounding plaza for Trump.

NBC News has reported that the Navy is discussing renaming an aircraft carrier, the USS Doris Miller, now under construction, for Trump. Miller grabbed an anti-aircraft gun during the attack on Pearl Harbor despite having no training on the weapon and is credited with having shot down at least one Japanese plane. Traditionally, warships are not named for sitting presidents.
In Palm Beach, Florida, home to Mar-a-Lago, the airport was recently renamed for the president. And yesterday, Trump joked the embattled Strait of Hormuz should be renamed the “Trump Strait.”

The White House has faced down a series of legal challenges to its projects.  And today, the administration announced it will begin excavation for the 250-foot-tall triumphal arch by the Arlington Memorial Bridge, taller than other iconic monuments including the Lincoln Memorial.
It all comes as NBC News reports that some Republicans are concerned these projects are distracting from what voters care about most: affordability.
Trump’s Cabinet on the campaign trail

Looking to cover maximum ground, members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet have been hitting the campaign trail ahead of the midterms to amplify his message.One who’s in particular demand is the health and human services secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“The MAHA voters are more attached to him than even to Trump, which is crazy,” said one GOP strategist who is involved in midterm races. “He’s one of the most requested Cabinet members” at campaign events.
Another Cabinet member who has shown up on the trail is Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which has raised eyebrows.

“I personally thought it was inappropriate for me to do that as a Cabinet official because my job was to build a consensus on Capitol Hill and in the country,” said William Cohen, a defense secretary under President Bill Clinton who had earlier served as a Republican senator from Maine. “If I were to go to a rally and speak on behalf of a given candidate, those who oppose that candidate would see that as me using the department.”
Asked for comment about Hegseth’s partisan political appearances, the Pentagon has said he makes those in his “personal capacity.”
“Department staff are not involved in, nor privy to, the details of events that Secretary Hegseth attends in his personal capacity,” a department official said. “Therefore, we have no comment.”

A Trump adviser said that the president’s political base reacts to Hegseth with an intensity that few other Trump surrogates can generate. Hegseth has told close friends and associates that he is considering a run for president in 2028, NBC News has reported. Hegseth, in a social media post after the article was published, said it was “100% false.”

“Pete Hegseth is loved by President Trump’s political base, and any time we can put people like him in front of those voters, it’s a good thing for Republicans,” the person, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said. “He gets them excited the way few can, and any criticism he receives for it only makes them love him more.”

title: DOJ asks Supreme Court to allow Trump’s USPS action on mail-in ballots to proceed ahead of midterm elections
summary: The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to green-light a new Postal Service rule that would exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections.
story: The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to green-light a new Postal Service rule that would exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections.
The appeal to the high court comes after U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani last week issued a temporary restraining order blocking parts of the rule from being implemented.

“With respect to the November 2026 election, the order thus partially nullifies the Postal Service’s efforts to address the risk that the federal mails will be used to perpetrate voter fraud, a particularly pernicious species of fraud that dilutes the votes of lawful voters, prevents election results from reflecting the will of the American people, and undermines ‘public confidence in the integrity of the electoral process,’” Solicitor General John Sauer wrote in the application.

While Talwani’s order “allows the Postal Service and the States to continue taking steps to ensure that their envelopes satisfy the rule’s requirements, the order risks sowing confusion and chaos because it makes those preparatory steps voluntary, rather than mandatory,” Sauer wrote.

There is a “grave risk,” Sauer writes, “that States may not have taken the necessary steps to comply due to the false sense of latitude created by the court’s improper order, potentially depriving those States’ citizens of the ability to vote by mail.”
It seeks an immediate stay of Talwani’s order while the case proceeds through the appeals court.

The timing of the request was unexpected, since the administration already had a pending appeal of the order to the First U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, and because Talwani was expected to rule Thursday on whether to issue a preliminary injunction in the case.

In her ruling last week, the judge sided with states and voting rights groups that claimed the rule unlawfully usurped states’ power to regulate their own elections, which is something that would need congressional approval, and left them facing an “impossible” timeline to comply in time for the November elections.

“Through the Final Rule, the USPS is refusing to send mail ballots to eligible voters unless States or local election officials submit their mail ballot envelopes and return envelopes and receive advance approval from the USPS without regard to impending deadlines for the November 3, 2026 election,” the judge wrote.

It also “requires elections officials to create accounts for a new electronic portal, certify that they have received approval regarding the mail ballot design, and thereafter upload to the USPS portal each voter’s information, including name, address, and a unique intelligent mail barcode,” she noted.

“Based on the record presently before the court, Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible as to the 2026 midterm elections, now little more than two months away,” Talwani wrote.

She said most states have already ordered their mail ballots “and some are required by state law to send them to eligible voters as early as next week.” North Carolina is scheduled to begin mailing out ballots Friday.

The states, she added, “have neither time nor funds to design new mail ballots, seek approval of the new designs, order production of mail ballots, update their own election management systems, train election officials to use the USPS portal, and upload citizen data to the portal, all before the midterms.”
While the government has said the measure is necessary to combat voter fraud, Talwani said it had not presented “any evidence regarding fraudulent absentee or mail-in voting.”

The “USPS’s interest in correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement of citizens who need access to mail ballots in order to vote,” she wrote.
The rule change came about as the result of an executive order issued by President Donald Trump on March 31 titled “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections.”

Talwani had signed off on an earlier order in a related case barring the rule from being implemented, but that ruling was overturned last month by the Supreme Court, which found her decision was premature because the rule had not yet been finalized.

“The court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the court said in an unsigned 6-3 ruling.
The rule was finalized late last month.
In court filings, the government said the changes that are being implemented are “modest.”

The rule simply turns “longstanding recommendations—which many of the Plaintiff States have already adopted at least in part, and some have long advocated for—into requirements,” the government argued.

It added that “this is ultimately a regulation of the U.S. mail, and a modest one at that—not a federal takeover of election administration by the Postal Service. That basic reality undermines virtually all of Plaintiffs’ claims and illustrates why Defendants are likely to succeed on the merits of their appeal.”

title: Former podcaster charged with threatening to kill Trump
summary: A former California podcaster has been arrested on charges he repeatedly threatened to kill the president.
story: A former California podcaster has been arrested on charges he repeatedly threatened to kill the president.

Benjamin Azariah Southworth, 40, of Los Angeles, engaged in repeated rants on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok in order “to publicly express his hatred toward President Trump and his supporters, and to publicly engage in and/or encourage the abuse, harassment and intimidation of, and violence against, President Trump,” prosecutors said in an indictment made public today.
He is expected to be arraigned Thursday in federal district court in Los Angeles, prosecutors added.

In one instance, Southworth posted a video “fictitiously depicting himself teleporting into the White House Oval Office, behind President Trump, and raising a knife up to President Trump’s head as if he was about to stab him,” the court filing said.
He also sold threatening merch on his website — stickers that said “Kill Trump,” according to prosecutors.
Southworth is the former host of the podcast “Yass, Jesus!” and a Christian reality show called “The Remix.”

He is additionally charged with cyberstalking and harassing one of the president’s personal attorneys and his family. The person was not named in the indictment, but FBI Director Kash Patel identified the victim as former Trump impeachment lawyer Jay Sekulow in a post on X.
“Deadly threats like this are as vile as they are criminal — those responsible will be met by this FBI and law enforcement,” Patel said in the post.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement about Southworth’s arrest that “We will hold perpetrators of violent threats accountable, and anyone who makes these threats online will not be allowed to hide behind their screens.”

title: Feds charge ICE officer with lying to investigators in the shooting of Venezuelan immigrant
summary: A federal grand jury returned an indictment against Christian Castro in the January shooting that left Julio Cesar Sosa Celis with a gunshot wound in one of his legs.
story: An ICE officer is facing federal charges for allegedly lying to federal investigators about the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant during immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis earlier this year.

A federal grand jury on Wednesday returned an indictment charging the officer, Christian Castro, with making false statements to the FBI about the Jan. 14 shooting that left Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis with a gunshot wound in his leg, a source familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
A separate investigation into whether Castro should face a more serious civil rights charge in the shooting is ongoing, the source added.
The Associated Press first reported on Castro’s latest federal charges.

The federal charges come a week after Castro was released from jail in Texas despite an extradition warrant from Minnesota prosecutors seeking his transfer. He’s facing state charges in Minnesota accusing him of assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.

Federal authorities had initially accused Sosa-Celis and another man of beating an immigration officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel in a confrontation that preceded the shooting, but federal prosecutors dropped the charges they filed against the men after video evidence showed the ICE officers may have lied about the encounter.

Castro was arrested in May in the Minnesota case. He was held in custody in Brownsville, Texas, until his release last week after a judge and Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign his extradition warrant — citing fraud investigations involving social services programs in Minnesota, which the Trump administration used to justify his immigration crackdown there.
Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary, told NBC News that “state law enforcement stands ready and willing to assist federal partners in facilitating Mr. Castro’s arrest if needed.”
Mahaleris added that “details of any federal indictment are best addressed to the U.S. Department of Justice.”
The Department of Homeland Security and the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office referred any queries to the DOJ.
An attorney for Castro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As news broke of Castro’s latest indictment, a federal prosecutor working on the case against Castro was fired, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Evans had told lawyers for Sosa-Celis that DOJ officials have blocked efforts to bring the more serious civil rights charge against Castro, ProPublica reported on Wednesday.
Evans did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and his DOJ email address returned an automated reply saying he was on leave.

title: Billionaire Leon Black sues House Oversight Committee over Epstein probe subpoenas
summary: Leon Black, a former Wall Street private equity investor, sued the House Oversight Committee, seeking to stop the panel from enforcing its subpoenas against him in an ongoing Epstein probe.
story: Leon Black, a former Wall Street private equity investor, on Thursday sued the House Oversight Committee, seeking to stop the panel from enforcing its subpoenas against him in an ongoing probe of the late disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

“The Committee is on a fishing expedition that oversteps its authority and completely ignores its responsibility. This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr. Black. We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power,” Black’s attorney, Susan Estrich, said in a statement.
Black had been set to appear before the committee Thursday morning.
The lawsuit comes after Black voluntarily sat for a closed-door transcribed interview with the Oversight Committee in late June but left the hearing early.

Lawmakers have for months sought more information on the financial web that allowed Epstein to fund his sex trafficking operation and whether Black was at all involved or aware of any illegal activity. They specifically have sought information about any nondisclosure agreements Black signed with women.
Black has denied any wrongdoing, involvement in or awareness of Epstein’s illegal activity.
In Thursday’s statement, she said that Black was “misled” about the intentions of the committee’s chair, Rep. James Comer, R-Ky.

“Mr. Black has cooperated with the Committee by voluntarily appearing to answer questions in a transcribed interview. Despite being misled about the intent of that interview, he then fully complied with the Committee’s subpoena related to Epstein,” Estrich said.
She added, “To imply misconduct because of the existence of a confidentiality agreement is entirely unjustified. Confidentiality agreements are routinely used in business.”

Estrich went on to wholly deny any allegations against Black, saying, “We want to reiterate that Mr. Black had no awareness of the criminal activities that led to Epstein’s arrest in 2019. Mr. Black never abused a woman. He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein.”

Black’s name appears more than 300 times in files released by the Justice Department late last year and early this year related to Epstein. His name appears often in emails from Epstein’s assistant, directing the financier to call Black. More than 100 of the mentions of Black are in emails from Epstein’s assistant, who wrote, “Leon Black returned your call.”

In a statement, Comer reacted to Black’s failure to appear before the committee Thursday, saying, “It’s a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people.”

He added, “Mr. Black’s testimony is crucial to our investigation as he was one of Mr. Epstein’s fee paying clients and has several non-disclosure agreements. Our deposition is moving forward this morning for the record and there will be an empty chair for Mr. Black. I will speak with our members about next steps.”
Black’s career and his reputation have been marred for years due to his relationship with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender who died in 2019.

In 2022, Black was sued over allegations that he raped a woman in Epstein’s New York City mansion in 2002. That case was later dropped with prejudice after both parties reached an agreement to do so and Black denied the allegations against him. A separate but ongoing lawsuit, filed in 2023, accused Black of raping a 16-year-old girl at Epstein’s Manhattan townhouse in 2002. A lawyer for Black denied the allegations, calling them “frivolous and sanctionable.” In April, a judge overseeing the case wrote that the plaintiff and her attorney “engaged in serious, sanctionable misconduct in this case,” but allowed the case to proceed.

Black in 2021 stepped down from the hedge fund he co-founded, Apollo Global Management, after the firm conducted an independent review looking into his ties to Epstein. The review found that Black was not involved in Epstein’s criminal activities.

Earlier this year, he was set to be deposed in a lawsuit filed by survivors of Epstein and his associates alleging that Bank of America facilitated and profited from Epstein’s illegal sex trafficking activity. Bank of America later settled that lawsuit for more than $70 million and did not admit any liability in that case.

“While we stand by our prior statements made in the filings in this case, including that Bank of America did not facilitate sex trafficking crimes, this resolution allows us to put this matter behind us and provides further closure for the plaintiffs,” a Bank of America spokesperson told NBC News at the time.

In a statement reacting to news of the lawsuit Thursday, Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said, “By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two Congressional subpoenas. Black gave Jeffrey Epstein over $180 million over six years. He funded Epstein’s abuse and trafficking of women. Multiple women have also accused Black of sexual assault. His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable.”
Garcia also called to hold Black in contempt of Congress.

title: OpenAI releases new model that it says triggered internal security measures
summary: The AI giant says its model better follows user intent and crosses a frontier for cybersecurity capabilities, and could be artificial general intelligence.
story: OpenAI released its newest and most powerful model, called GPT-6 Astra, Thursday to a limited set of customers, labelling it the world’s most intelligent AI system and the first model to trigger advanced internal safety protections given its cyber capabilities.

The company said the model sets a new high-water mark for its ability to autonomously control computer systems and perform tasks on behalf of users, such as filling out spreadsheets and  creating websites from scratch.
“Astra can really do anything a human can do with a computer,” OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said before the model was released.

Brockman said that Astra represented a “jump” in capabilities for its AI systems and said it would be reasonable to see Astra as a version of artificial general intelligence (AGI), often referred to as AI systems that can perform most meaningful tasks as well as humans. “Welcome to the AGI era!” Brockman said.

The company also emphasized that the model is faster and more efficient than its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol, on a variety of tasks. For example, OpenAI said that Astra achieved a higher score using fewer output tokens, a common unit of measurement for AI tasks, on a key cybersecurity test called ExploitGym.
“Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browser use, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing Astra’s release.

OpenAI said Astra would first be made available to participants in its Daybreak program for cybersecurity defenders, with wider access for enterprise and consumer accounts planned for the coming days.

Astra’s release comes just days after rival Anthropic released its latest models, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, which it said set its own new frontiers for a range of scientific, coding and reasoning tasks.

Both companies said their respective models were world-leading AI systems. OpenAI called Astra “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model.” Rival Anthropic crowned its own systems as “the world’s most advanced models for coding and knowledge work.”
Astra’s release comes amid rising concerns and scrutiny about frontier AI companies’ cybersecurity protocols and ability to control their own technology.

In a report released last week, OpenAI said that a model in the same family as Astra that was not meant for public release managed to autonomously establish administrator control over part of OpenAI’s own infrastructure and potentially exposed secret OpenAI information to the open internet.
The company said this activity, along with other “misaligned” behavior, happened without the knowledge of its staff members, despite some internal efforts to monitor AI agents.
“As these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” said Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, on Thursday.

On Tuesday, OpenAI said that Astra was its first model to cross certain internal capability thresholds for implementing stricter security measures, as laid out in its longstanding Preparedness Framework.

Astra “can find previously unknown security flaws and develop ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step,” the company wrote in a Tuesday blog post. OpenAI said it rolled out increased cybersecurity protocols over the past several weeks.
The company said Astra will feature increased monitoring mechanisms, so OpenAI can “rapidly detect and contain potentially misaligned actions.”
However, Pachocki said that current techniques for monitoring and observing models’ behavior may not hold, as AI systems become more advanced and potentially evade human monitors’ oversight.
He said the company takes this loss of oversight and insight seriously, and that it would factor into its future development decisions.
“We will not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We will withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence,” he said.

On Tuesday, The Information reported that a training technique involved in Astra’s development could drastically decrease humans’ ability to understand how the AI system “thinks” or processes user commands.
The report triggered a firestorm of online criticism about decreased safety protocols. Pachocki pushed back on that reporting, writing on X that he wanted “to prevent a race into unmonitorability.”

Despite growing challenges in overseeing AI systems’ behavior, OpenAI also said that Astra better follows and understands user intent, while less frequently trying to cheat or work around internal protections compared to GPT-5.6 Sol.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that Astra also went through the White House’s voluntary vetting process for cutting-edge AI systems, telling Axios on Wednesday that “of course” the company decided to let the administration review Astra.

Brockman said the White House did not request any substantial changes to Astra. “There is nothing that they came back with saying that you need to change this in terms of safeguards,” he said Thursday.

Many AI experts and members of Congress are clamoring for more visibility into the exact way the White House and federal offices involved with AI, including the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and the National Security Agency, test advanced AI systems before they are released to the public.

title: Arrest warrant issued for ‘Below Deck Mediterranean’ star Nathan Gallagher
summary: Australian police have issued an arrest warrant for “Below Deck Mediterranean” star Nathan Gallagher after he missed a court appearance related to an alleged domestic violence incident.
story: Australian police have issued an arrest warrant for “Below Deck Mediterranean” star Nathan Gallagher after he missed a court appearance related to an alleged domestic violence incident.

New South Wales police shared a photo of Gallagher, 28, and asked the public for help locating him. He is known to frequent the Emington and Melrose Park areas but is “believed to be offshore,” authorities said in a news release, which notes he has outstanding warrants in Sydney. In a Facebook post, police warned the public not to approach him if spotted.
The reality star, from Burtonport, Ireland, works as a deckhand on the Bravo series. He was arrested on domestic violence charges in December 2025, NBC Los Angeles reported.
Gallagher was granted conditional bail. He was due back in court Tuesday but never appeared, according to the station.
In a statement to Rolling Stone in August, Gallagher acknowledged he has “made mistakes,” but said he didn’t think “the public has heard the full story surrounding what happened.”

Police have not named the alleged victim, but Rolling Stone reported that Gallagher’s statement pointed to his former partner and “Below Deck” cast member Gael Cameron. He called the situation “extremely complicated.”

“I’m not claiming I was perfect. I wasn’t. I made mistakes and I will take responsibility for my own actions. But I will not accept being portrayed solely through one person’s account of a relationship when there is another side and evidence relating to it,” he told Rolling Stone.
Gallagher added his biggest concern was his son, whom he shares with Cameron.
“Below Deck Mediterranean” is currently airing its 11th season.
The current season wrapped production before the December incident, Bravo said.
“Bravo does not plan on working with Nathan in the future,” a spokesperson said in a statement.
Cameron did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday.

title: Fox News parts ways with Maria Bartiromo
summary: Fox News has parted ways with longtime anchor Maria Bartiromo, a vocal defender of President Donald Trump who hosted several financial news shows.
story: Fox News said Thursday that it had parted ways with longtime anchor Maria Bartiromo, a vocal defender of President Donald Trump who hosted several financial news shows.
“We thank Maria for her work over the lasts 12½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter,” a spokesperson said in a statement that did not elaborate further.

Bartiromo has been Fox Business Network’s global markets editor since joining it in 2014. She hosted “Mornings with Maria” and “Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street” on Fox Business, while also anchoring “Sunday Morning Futures,” a business-focused show on Fox News Channel.
Bartiromo joined Fox from CNBC, where she hosted one of the network’s highest-profile programs, “Closing Bell” and was the first person to report live from the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.
Bartiromo’s departure was “effective today,” said the Fox spokesperson.

Bartiromo built a reputation as a trailblazer for women in financial media and television broadcasting. She drew attention in media circles for taking a more openly conservative turn in her reporting after leaving CNBC, where her work had been largely apolitical.
Many of Trump’s Cabinet secretaries appeared regularly on her shows during both of his terms in office. Fox also regularly touted Bartiromo’s shows as ratings winners.

In 2021, Bartiromo’s comments and shows were cited as exhibits in a defamation lawsuit filed by the voting machine maker Dominion Voting Systems against Fox News. Dominion alleged that the cable network operator had knowingly broadcast false claimed that Dominion had rigged the 2020 presidential election.
Fox News and Dominion eventually settled the lawsuit in 2023 for $787 million.
During her nearly 21 years at CNBC, Bartiromo appeared regularly on national broadcast programs, including NBC’s “TODAY” and “Nightly News” during the 2007-2008 financial crisis.
Comcast, the parent company of NBC News, spun off CNBC in 2025.
Bartiromo did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on her departure.
Bartiromo has not appeared on FBN’s air since Aug. 9, according to a review of archived episodes of her shows. Her biography page and show pages had already been removed from Fox’s websites Thursday.
Bartiromo was one of the first financial journalists on cable TV whose influence extended beyond Wall Street.
Early in her career, Bartiromo had been dubbed the “Money Honey,” a nickname she later said she had misgivings about.
In the early 1990s, The Ramones’ Joey Ramone released a song titled “Maria Bartiromo.”
She also appeared in the 2010 film “Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps,” where she played herself alongside Michael Douglas’ Gordon Gekko in a scene set at a fictional CNBC interview.

title: Probe finds Dianna Russini’s ties to Patriots coach to be ‘awkward’ and ‘uncomfortable’
summary: The Athletic found its former NFL reporter Dianna Russini wrote in an “awkward” and “uncomfortable” manner about coach Mike Vrabel — based on a relationship with him that she should’ve disclosed, the New York Times-owned digital sports publication said Thursday.
story: The Athletic found its former NFL reporter Dianna Russini wrote in an  “awkward” and “uncomfortable” manner about coach Mike Vrabel — based on a relationship with him that she should’ve disclosed, the New York Times-owned digital sports publication said Thursday.

However, Mike Semel, The Athletic’s editorial director for standards and quality, who led the probe into Russini’s work, said he did not uncover “clear” evidence that the publication’s one-time NFL insider wrongly propped up Vrabel’s professional interests.
Russini resigned from The Athletic in April, less than a week after photos of she and the married Vrabel, 51, at an Arizona hotel drew scrutiny.
“I’ve not found a clear link to conclude that Russini used her platform to help promote Vrabel or help his teams during her time at The Athletic,” Semel wrote in a piece published Thursday.
“That said, there are examples of Russini writing glowingly of Vrabel that in hindsight are awkward or even uncomfortable.”

Semel said he “reviewed 903 stories and 77 videos published on The Athletic site and app that carried Russini’s byline, co-byline, a contributor line or a mention of her reporting” in addition to “204 episodes of the Scoop City podcast, produced by The Athletic and co-hosted by Russini.”
Semel also looked over “25 off-platform appearances or interviews for which she was in some way representing The Athletic and interviewed 14 Athletic staffers.
Semel’s piece did not mention any interviews with Russini herself for this probe.
Russini, 43, could not be immediately reached for comment on Thursday.

“Russini’s relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic’s standards,” according to Semel. “Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed.”

In addition to several gushing comments Russini has made about Vrabel on various platforms, Semel zeroed in on a 2023 “What I’m Hearing” column, in which she wrote that Vrabel, then head coach of the Tennessee Titans, wouldn’t be fired.

“Angry Tennessee Titans fans can stop hoping owner Amy Adams Strunk fires Vrabel. It’s not happening. Based on multiple conversations with high-ranking Titans officials, the franchise strongly and collectively believes it has the right coach for long-term success,” according to Russini.
The Titans fired Vrabel two months later.

Vrabel returned to coaching in 2025 and led New England to one of the greatest turnarounds in recent NFL history. The 2025 coach of the year, Vrabel took a squad, which had gone 4-13 in consecutive campaigns, to a 14-3 mark and AFC title this past season.

title: Oil touches $97 per barrel as diesel prices surge to highest level this year
summary: The price of crude oil rose on Thursday, part of a monthlong run that has helped push the average cost of diesel fuel to its highest level since 2022.
story: A monthlong run of rising crude oil prices and refineries nearing capacity has pushed the average cost of diesel fuel to its highest level since 2022.
At $5.78 per gallon on Thursday, the cost of diesel is up more than 53% since the war with Iran started in late February. At the time, diesel averaged $3.76 per gallon nationwide.

The price of unleaded gasoline, which most personal vehicles run on, rose alongside diesel Thursday. According to AAA data tracked by NBC News, the national average was $4.14 per gallon, up two cents from Wednesday.

title: From Jane Fonda to Miss Piggy, Celebrities Share Moving Tributes To Gloria Steinem
summary: Tributes are pouring in from celebrities across an array of fields for the trailblazing feminist icon Gloria Steinem, who died Sept. 2.
story: Tributes are pouring in from celebrities across an array of fields for the trailblazing feminist icon Gloria Steinem, who died Sept. 2.

Prominent voices across sports, entertainment and more have shared emotional words about the impact that the journalist and activist, who dedicated her life to championing women’s rights, had on their lives and the greater movement towards gender equality. The messages follow Steinem’s passing, “surrounded by some of the many who loved her,” according to an announcement shared on her official Instagram account.

“She had a clever, often funny way to say just what was needed to surface feelings and ideas about where we belonged, what our inchoate yearnings meant, whether power was a word that women could and should embrace for ourselves, and how different power looked when held in men’s hands alone,” actor and fellow outspoken women’s rights activist Jane Fonda, who co-founded the Women’s Media Center with Steinem and writer Robin Morgan, wrote in an Instagram post.
Fonda added that Steinem “lives on in the changed lives of many women who don’t consider themselves feminists or part of the women’s movement.”

“I’ve met many such women who because of what Gloria said or wrote gained the courage to leave bad marriages, start their own businesses, persuade husbands to help with household chores,” Fonda said in the post.
Steinem died “peacefully at her home in New York City,” according to the Instagram post shared on her official account. She was 92.

During her decades in the spotlight, Steinem left a significant cultural imprint on American society. And today, she is largely considered one of the faces of the second-wave of feminism — one that broadened the fight for equal rights from a focus on the right to vote to also include issues like employment, politics, education and sexuality.

Skyrocketing to national prominence in 1963, Steinem made a name for herself after going undercover as a Playboy bunny and publishing a two-part exposé on the working conditions and treatment of women at the controversial New York Playboy Club. In 1971, she launched the groundbreaking feminist outlet Ms. magazine, which became one of the first women-led publications to tackle heavy issues like domestic violence and abortion.

For decades, Steinem continued her work, co-founding several other organizations including the National Women’s Political Caucus, the Women’s Action Alliance and the Ms. Foundation for Women along with the Women’s Media Center.
From television host Andy Cohen to the fabulous Muppet queen Miss Piggy, celebrities honored the outspoken activist for her undeniable contributions to society.
Here’s a look at how prominent figures across industries are mourning Steinem’s death and celebrating her legacy.
Jane Fonda
Fonda, who collaborated with Steinem for decades, shared details of the late activist’s life, including the way in which she “built the new women’s movement.”

“Gloria, in her graceful, kind, and deeply intelligent way, changed the world we live in,” Fonda wrote. “For decades, she trudged through every airport in the country, in sandals and a trench, carrying her own suitcase, packed with a few black clothes, hair curlers, and steam iron, in order to speak to women — at conferences, town halls, consciousness raising groups. No group was too small to deserve Gloria’s time.”
Lena Dunham
Writer and “Girls” creator Lena Dunham shared personal memories she had of the activist, including some particularly moving anecdotes on how Steinem took her under her wing.

“You let me wander in as a lost twenty something, determined that things should change and unsure how or if they could, and you advised me on everything from men (can be fun, aren’t required) to activism (it’s a marathon, not a race.),” Dunham recalled.
Miss Piggy

The iconic Muppet Miss Piggy posted an emotional message on Instagram in remembrance of Steinem, whom she shared a evening of conversation during the 2015 Sackler Center First Awards. That night, Miss Piggy was honored as a feminist icon herself.

“Throughout her incredible life, Gloria broke glass ceilings, challenged perceptions, and fiercely advocated for women around the world,” Piggy wrote. “Few people have inspired and influenced moi more than dear Gloria, and I will forever treasure the fabulous times we shared together.”
Oprah
Oprah Winfrey shared post on Instagram, recounting a 2012 event in which the two spoke to young women at Barnard College.
“I was proud to bear witness to their sense of worthiness and independence—and recognized how Gloria’s work had helped forge the path to that moment,” she wrote.
Winfrey also mentioned that Steinem “leaves us with more freedom than she inherited and with the responsibility to keep widening that freedom for the women and girls who come next.”
Billie Jean King

Tennis icon Billie Jean King, who was featured in the first version of Ms. magazine, shared on social media that the world “has lost a true giant and a dynamic voice.” King, whose 1973 win against Bobby Riggs in the “Battle of the Sexes” match became a symbol of women’s empowerment, praised Steinem for her indefatigable spirit.
“She devoted her life to the pursuit of equality and political change, working tirelessly for over 70 years to ensure each generation built upon the work of the previous one,” King wrote.
Meghan Markle

The former Meghan Markle, whose official title is Duchess of Sussex, shared a post on Instagram about Steinem, whom she considered a “friend and mentor.” Markle, whose highly publicized marriage to Prince Harry has long been the subject of tabloid fodder, shared that Steinem had a close relationship with her family and often helped her during difficult times.

“Publicly, we did interviews together, called young voters to encourage them to have their voices heard, attended award ceremonies, and brainstormed how to help this beautiful yet complicated world to become more equitable,” Markle recalled in her post.

She added that “privately, she was even better than you would imagine- spending Thanksgiving with our family, introducing me to one of my best friends (forever the champion of female friendship), loving our children with her whole heart, counseling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit.”
Andy Cohen

Bravo icon Andy Cohen shared a hilarious story about how he once invited Steinem to his talk show “Watch What Happens Live” in 2015 to discuss the reality show personalities in his “Real Housewives” franchise. And he had a pretty perfect description of not only what went down, but also of the activist.
“She absolutely ATE ME ALIVE,” he joked. “What an incredible human with a legacy that will outlive us all.

title: Ms. Magazine Pays Tribute To Gloria Steinem, Its Revolutionary Founder
summary: As the world honors trailblazing feminist, journalist and activist Gloria Steinem, who died this week, the groundbreaking magazine she founded more than a half century ago has paid tribute to the icon.
story: As the world honors trailblazing feminist, journalist and activist Gloria Steinem, who died this week, the groundbreaking magazine she founded more than a half century ago has paid tribute to the icon.

Ms. magazine, which Steinem launched in the 1970s as an answer to a media landscape that largely catered to male interests and relegated women to lifestyle issues, published a moving obituary about the revolutionary founder. It comes hours after it was announced that Steinem had died Sept. 2 in her New York City home, according to a post on her official Instagram page. She was 92.
In the obituary, executive editor Kathy Spillar wrote about the ways in which Steinem “transformed journalism, feminism and the possibilities women could imagine for themselves.”

“For more than half a century, the public knew her as one of feminism’s most recognizable figures: the writer with the center-parted hair and aviator glasses; the assured speaker at rallies, campuses and conventions; the tireless traveler who carried the movement’s ideas into living rooms and union halls, onto television screens and into the corridors of political power,” Spillar wrote in the tribute published Sept. 3. “But Steinem understood something the culture surrounding her often did not: Movements are never made by one person.”

Steinem “passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her,” according to the Instagram post on her official page. The post did not give a cause of death.

Her women-run magazine, which released its first standalone issue in 1972, continues to publish in print as well as digitally. And much like it did at its inception, the outlet covers stories ranging from women’s health, democracy and culture.

Spillar, who helms the publication, wrote in the tribute that Steinem, who tirelessly championed causes ranging from reproductive rights to eradicating workplace inequalities, fought to elevate intersectionality in the women’s movement.

“She insisted that feminism’s history include the Black women, labor organizers, Indigenous women, lesbians, civil rights leaders and community activists whose work had too often been erased,” Spillar wrote, adding that Steinem often credited figures of all backgrounds —  including Shirley Chisolm, the first Black woman to be elected to the United States Congress and civil rights leader and voting rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer — as influences and teachers.

Spillar added that when “the media attempted to anoint her the leader of a leaderless movement, she redirected attention toward the organizers, coalitions and collective action that made change possible.”

Steinem first rose to national prominence in 1963 after going undercover as a Playboy bunny and producing a two-part exposé on the working conditions and treatment of women at the infamous New York Playboy Club.

“The investigation made her famous, but it also temporarily made editors less willing to take her seriously,” Spillar wrote. “That experience taught Steinem a lasting lesson about who determines which stories count as news, and about the cost women pay when men control the institutions that assign, edit, finance and distribute those stories.”

In 1971, Steinem started Ms. as an insert in New York Magazine. At the time, the media environment was heavily skewed toward male consumers, Steinem said, and that there were “no other magazines for women that weren’t about food, fashion and family.”

“I believed that advertisers would soon realize that women’s interests were just as wide and deep as men’s interests are and there would be new magazines that were at least like, say, Esquire for women,” she wrote in a 2023 book about the magazine in celebration of its 50th anniversary.

The insert found almost instant success and sold 300,000 copies in under one week. It contained rarely covered topics from domestic violence to abortion. The groundbreaking preview also included a list of women, including Steinem herself, who admitted to having abortions before they were federally legalized through 1973’s Roe v. Wade decision. The list featured names from Anaïs Nin to Billie Jean King.

The preview itself was highly controversial. CBS “60 Minutes” host Harry Reasoner, for example, famously said, “I’ll give it six months before they run out of things to say.” Years later, Reasoner apologized for the remark.
